articles.title: In Pursuit of the Status Quo: ASWB’s Research, Grantmaking, and Regulatory Practices
articles.abstract: The Association of Social Work Boards (ASWB) Examination Program is used in all 50 states to regulate the practice of clinical social work and in the majority of states to regulate the practice of masters and bachelors-level social work. After releasing descriptive data demonstrating biases in exam pass rates by race, age, and dominant language, ASWB engaged in research and regulatory actions that violate social work ethics and psychometric best practices. This article will critique the research, grantmaking, and regulatory practices that support the ASWB Examination Program using extensive citations to psychometric standards, ASWB’s publications and exam documentation, and the researchers’ experiences engaging with ASWB to study the cause of exam score disparities. The analysis will reveal how, after their 2022 release of data demonstrating exam bias with respect to race, age, and language, ASWB funded researchers already affiliated with ASWB to support what it already tells test-takers in its exam guidebook–only structural factors bias exam scores, not psychometric flaws internal to the examination. Moreover, ASWB implemented solutions to exam bias without proper investigation and psychometric support. Because of ASWB’s position as the sole publisher and purchaser of licensing examinations, individual state boards are unable to make incremental changes to prevent biased ASWB examinations from closing the profession of social work to groups for whom the exam is invalid, unreliable, and unfair.

articles.title: Uniquely Biased: How ASWB Exams Violate Psychometric Best Practices
articles.abstract: After publication of the 2022 Pass Rate Analysis demonstrating minoritized social workers pass at less than half the rate of White social workers, the Association of Social Work Board (ASWB) Examination Guidebook (ASWB, 2023a), revised its psychometric reporting of exam fairness from “statistically free of race and gender bias” to “differences in exam performance for…different demographic groups…is influenced by many factors external to the exam,” upstream of the examination in the workforce pipeline (p. 9). Focusing only on factors external to the exam ignores the possibility that the internal properties of the exam may be invalid, unreliable, and unfair. Race, class, culture, and other structural factors do not impact ASWB exams the same over time, with ASWB’s 2022 Exam Pass Rate Analysis reporting 10-13% reductions in bachelors and masters examination pass rates after the introduction of the 2018 exam blueprint. Using extensive references to ASWB’s public statements, this article will demonstrate how ASWB ignored evidence of examination flaws and presents external factors as the only possible explanation for disparities in pass rates. Beginning with the policy paradox created by national organizational disagreement on the cause and next steps on exam score inequities, this article will review the extant empirical evidence demonstrating how bias is encoded to the language and theories underlying the examination as well as psychometric shortcomings in ASWB’s exam validation process converge to create a uniquely biased exam.

articles.title: Early-Career Research Funding Predicts Success in Scientific Careers: A Mathematical Model and Empirical Analysis of Matthew Effects
articles.abstract: Success breeds success. This simple idea—the Matthew effect, or cumulative advantage—is a classical theme in the science of science. Does obtaining a research grant very early in a researcher’s career, at the very beginning of their academic trajectory, create a performance gap that continues to widen for decades? We approach this question from two sides. First, we build a mathematical model in which talent, publications, research funding, and promotion mutually reinforce one another, and show that even when talent is held constant, the gap in research output between early grant recipients and non-recipients widens over time. We distil this prediction into two hypotheses. Second, we test these hypotheses using a large panel dataset of approximately 40,000 researchers spanning eight broad fields of Japanese academia, drawn from the researchmap database. Using the graduate school of origin as a proxy for talent and prestige, we find that the advantage associated with receiving an early-career fellowship remains positive, statistically significant, and steadily increases over time even after accounting for differences in the institution of origin. In short, even a head start lasting only a few years leaves a lasting mark on a researcher’s career, with its effects continuing to grow more than a decade later. By combining an explicit model of cumulative advantage with large-scale empirical evidence across fields, we quantify how the earliest allocation of research resources shapes the long-term stratification of science.

articles.title: Contextualising Urban Change: A Novel Classification System for Measuring Built Environment Change Across Great Britain
articles.authors: Jess Hepburn, Fiona Caryl, Rich Mitchell, Richard Patterson, Laura Macdonald, Alexandros Sfyridis, Daniela Fecht, Jenna Panter
articles.abstract: Public health policy increasingly recognises the influence of built environments on health outcomes. However, most spatial datasets cannot track context-dependent environmental changes over time, a critical limitation when assessing the health impacts of urban development. This study develops the Built Environment Context and Change Atlas (BECCA), a novel methodology quantifying context-dependent built environment changes across Great Britain (2015-2020). Using the best available national spatial data, we integrated information on buildings, roads, and land cover, applying multivariate clustering to classify both environmental context and changes at 500m resolution. Stakeholders guided the definition of meaningful change categories. BECCA identified that 11% of GB cells underwent change, with substantial variation in development patterns across Functional Urban Areas, ranging from peripheral expansion to infill growth. While developed for Great Britain, this methodological framework is adaptable to other national contexts with similar spatial data availability, offering a template for international environmental change monitoring. By addressing critical gaps in existing environmental change data, BECCA provides a robust foundation for future research linking built environment dynamics to health outcomes, supporting evidence-based urban planning decisions.

articles.title: Watching the walls go up: r/wallstreetbets segregated after the GameStop squeeze
articles.abstract: Online communities keep ideas apart. Across Hacker News and Reddit, concept pairs that should co-occur but never have stay apart at rates far below chance. We call this a wall. The exception was r/wallstreetbets: at chance before 2020, walled by 2024 like everywhere else. Here we report a registered study of when that happened, using rolling quarterly windows over a fresh single-source corpus of 98.1 million Reddit posts and comments, 2019 to 2024. Three predictions committed in advance all pass. The community moves from chance-level mixing to persistent walls, onset 2021-04-01, with zero reversions. In the two windows straddling the January 2021 GameStop episode, suppressed ticker pairs co-mention 28.6 and 30.9 standard deviations above chance. It is the only above-chance excursion this research program has observed, and shuffled data never produce it. Analysis-oriented control communities stay walled through the squeeze, so the excursion is specific to r/wallstreetbets. Two causes were in play, thirty-fold growth during the squeeze and a moderation overhaul after it, and we decided in advance that a mid-2021 onset could point to either. Segregation transitions in online communities can be measured and dated, but their timing alone cannot identify the mechanisms behind them.

articles.title: Ideas that never meet online mark divided communities, not future discoveries
articles.abstract: In science, two well-studied ideas never discussed together make a likely candidate for a future discovery. Predicting which pair connects next is the aim of literature-based discovery. Whether this holds in online discussion is untested. Here we test it on 200 thousand Hacker News discussions from 2015 to 2017, with a pre-registered replication on 41.5 million Reddit finance posts, 2017 to 2024, using stock tickers. Four pre-registered evaluations use threads, then authors, as documents. Pairs never discussed together, called suppressed pairs, connect no more than popularity and overlapping topics predict. On the Science4Cast benchmark of AI papers, where the effect is known, the same method finds it. The standard test against chance flags connections too easily when document sizes vary. It reported 19 to 24 percent of pairs connecting within authors' quarterly output, yet shuffled data connected more pairs than real data. A per-pair permutation test leaves new connections no higher than false positives produce. Suppressed pairs appear together far below chance: nearly 9 standard deviations at author level, over 100 at thread level. Both results replicate across the 2020-2021 market regime change. Ideas that never meet online mark communities that stay apart, not future discoveries waiting to happen.

articles.title: Well-intended policy gone wrong? Voluntary Surrenders as a de facto amnesty for illegal wildlife use and trade in Colombia
articles.authors: Natalia Munoz Cassolis, Johana M. Herrera Montoya, Douglas MacMillan, Francisco Perera Rieder, Melissa Arias
articles.abstract: The illegal wildlife trade (IWT) has been the focus of numerous international and national legal frameworks aiming to counter the harms it poses to biodiversity. The enforcement of these laws typically involves the seizure or confiscation of wildlife specimens, which have become a common metric for IWT reporting and a proxy for estimating its scale. Another commonly used, but less understood mechanism is the Voluntary Surrender of wildlife specimens. Our research examines the legal implications and practical implementation of Voluntary Surrenders in Colombia, where this administrative mechanism was originally designed as a transitional educational tool to raise awareness of the environmental and welfare harms of illegal wildlife pet keeping, and to encourage individuals to relinquish illegally held specimens. Drawing on a thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with environmental legal experts, law enforcement officers, and conservation researchers and practitioners, we identified the typologies of actors and circumstances giving rise to Voluntary Surrenders, alongside the legal interpretation, implementation, and governance challenges linked to this mechanism. We demonstrate how this well-intentioned policy operates as a de facto amnesty for IWT in Colombia, enabling offenders to evade sanctions and law enforcement personnel to bypass burdensome sanctioning procedures. Consequently, Voluntary Surrenders have perpetuated impunity, normalized illicit wildlife possession, reinforced a notion of IWT as a non-serious crime, and obscured its true scale, as these incidents are systematically excluded from national and international reporting frameworks, such as the CITES Illegal Trade database. We conclude that an urgent revision of this regulatory framework is needed.

articles.title: AI in Science and its Implications: A Narrative Review
articles.authors: Philip Shapira, John Nelson, Julie Jebsen, Seoyoon Kang
articles.abstract: This narrative review synthesizes diverse empirical, technical, conceptual, and policy literature on the development and use of AI in science. Drawing on a sociology of science and technology framing, we examine how the adoption of AI may redistribute scientific work, expertise, epistemic authority, resources, and accountability across organizational and infrastructural contexts. The literature suggests three cross-cutting patterns. First, AI tends to redistribute rather than eliminate work, creating new demands for configuration, monitoring, interpretation, and validation. Second, gains in productivity and novelty are uneven and depend on problem characteristics, data, infrastructure, and complementary human expertise. Third, AI may shift authority and institutional power toward actors that develop, own, and govern models and computational resources. AI also raises contested questions about explanation, evidence, creativity, responsibility, inequality, and environmental costs. We identify priorities for research on the epistemic status of AI-generated knowledge, inequalities in access to infrastructure and training, disciplinary variations, changing forms of accountability and institutional authority, and the governance of AI in and for science.

articles.title: Correcting molecular myopia in chemical risk governance: hormonal infrastructure as a conceptual lens
articles.abstract: Widespread declines in human fecundity and biodiversity signal a creeping crisis that links to proliferating chemical pollution. Problematically, the risk governance of chemicals is mired with laboratory-level molecular knowledge that poorly matches with population-level threats arising from cumulative, chronic exposures to multiple borderline toxicants. We identify this molecular myopia as a fundamental misalignment between the scales at which chemical governance operates and the scales at which ecotoxicological research raises alarm—a misalignment reproduced in ongoing EU regulatory reforms despite their protective ambitions. In this conceptual work, we apply institutional theory and science and technology studies to explicate the key role of scale alignment in enabling effective governance intervention. Focusing on endocrine-disrupting chemicals, we develop the concept of hormonal infrastructure to highlight the cultural-cognitive level from which scale realignment must begin with chemical governance. This infrastructural lens foregrounds hormonal functions as vital and shared ecologies that require distributed human care to withstand diffuse chemical pollution. By reframing chemical risks as policy objects through infrastructures rather than through molecules, we make the case for a more prudential and multilevel form of precaution to address multichemical exposures that continue to slip through regulatory oversight.

articles.title: The Accountability Gap in Sub-Sovereign ESG Finance: A Case Study of Police Administration Oversight in Chiba Prefecture, Japan

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This paper examines a critical vulnerability in the methodology of sub-sovereign ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) ratings, utilizing Chiba Prefecture, Japan, as a primary case study. While global ESG frameworks increasingly evaluate local government bonds, rating agencies predominantly rely on macro-level socioeconomic indicators and overarching policy frameworks, creating a significant "measurement gap." We demonstrate how this macro-dependence obscures micro-level governance failures—specifically, the indefinite suspension of complaint processing and the systemic non-creation of official records within police administration. By applying an axiomatic approach grounded in administrative law and corporate governance principles, this study empirically documents the existence of a structural "Accountability Gap" at the operational entry point. The findings highlight the critical need for institutional investors and ESG rating agencies to discount the reliability of sub-sovereign sustainability representations when auditable management evidence is structurally absent.

articles.title: Exchangeable Versus Age- structured Priors in Small-Area Estimation of Adult Mortality From Sibling Survival Histories
articles.authors: Shorful Alam, Nazmul Haque, Abdul Mazed, Md Foysal Ahmed
articles.abstract: Sibling survival histories provide adult mortality estimates for countries lacking civil registration, but age-sex disaggregation often leaves cells sparse. Analysts routinely smooth these estimates using either an exchangeable prior, which borrows strength across all cells, or an age-structured prior, which borrows from neighboring ages, a choice rarely justified explicitly. We compared empirical Bayes, Bayesian IID, and age-structured (RW2) smoothing of visibility-corrected estimates from the 2024 Nigeria and 2016 Nepal Demographic and Health Surveys, chosen for contrasting sparsity (37–93 versus 8–30 effective deaths per cell), plus a simulation under known ground truth. In Nigeria's denser cells, the two priors agreed closely; in Nepal's sparser cells, six of 14 diverged materially, four female age groups showed nominally significant divergence, and three remained significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons. Raw sparsity did not predict which cells diverged: simulations show divergence instead reflects genuine local departures from the broader age pattern, which age-structured priors recover more faithfully than exchangeable priors, at a modest cost that includes spreading artificial input distortions to neighboring cells. Empirical Bayes intervals also badly undercovered when the true pattern was smooth. We recommend routine reporting of exchangeable-versus-structured divergence as a standard part of small-area demographic estimation.

articles.title: Czech Women Scientists and Their Career Development in the Course of ‘Two Regimes’, 1968– 2018: Case Study for the Natural Sciences
articles.abstract: Czech society still needs to improve the low representation of women in science, especially in middle and higher management positions and some fields, typically technical or natural sciences. The article aims to uncover some aspects of this development’s historical contexts using the example of female scientists’ career building during two regimes (1968–2004), i.e., the period of state socialism before 1989 and the democratic market environment after 1989. The study reveals the persistent impact of gender stereotypes and barriers in the field, with an emphasis on women’s maternal role. Work-life balance, if it is not sufficiently supported (by institutions or individuals, typically partners), thus becomes an effective inhibitor for women’s scientific careers. With analysis and interpretation of personal narratives, the study focuses on the development and path dependency of this phenomenon. It offers an understanding of the longterm context of the current undervalued representation of women in science management.

articles.title: ALFRED MARSHALL AND SOCIALISM: NOBLE ENDS, FLAWED MEANS, OR SO THE ECONOMIST SAYS
articles.abstract: This article revisits Alfred Marshall’s nuanced perspective on socialism by pairing a reconstruction from primary sources (the Lectures on Socialism & the Function of Government transcribed from the manuscript in folder 3/16 of the Marshall Library included) with a systematic reading of the secondary literature. Marshall’s objections to modern and utopian socialisms turn on incentives, price determination and organizational adaptability and not, at least not explicitly, on a rejection of socialist aims. What emerges is that Marshall’s criticisms, diagnosing informational and incentive failures in collectivist schemes, coexist with a moral concern for his view of progress in capabilities and living standards.

articles.title: Compensability in composite lifestyle and well-being indices: a simulation study of power-mean aggregation
articles.authors: Aamir Saeed Malik, Ahmed H. Hassan, Waqas Rasheed, Shahid Bashir
articles.abstract: Composite indices of well-being and health almost always combine domain scores using an unweighted arithmetic mean. This choice permits unlimited compensation between domains: a high score in one domain can wholly offset a collapsed score in another. Whether that is appropriate depends on what the index is for, yet the choice is rarely stated as a choice. We examine its consequences for a five-domain lifestyle index, comparing four members of the power-mean family across four data-generating mechanisms in a Monte Carlo study of 100,000 profiles, reported following the ADEMP structure. Three findings follow. First, the arithmetic mean has a uniform gradient: every domain returns the same marginal gain, so the operator supplies no ordering over which domain to improve. Non-compensatory operators identify the weakest domain with probability one. Second, the arithmetic mean permits substantial masking: where one domain has collapsed below 50, between 4.7% and 35.9% of such profiles still score at or above the conventional adequacy threshold of 70, against 0.2% to 9.5% under the harmonic mean. Third, disagreement is concentrated, not general: rankings agree closely for correlated, mostly high scores but diverge sharply for imbalanced profiles. Aggregation therefore encodes a normative judgement about substitutability. Which operator to use follows from purpose: the arithmetic mean to summarise attainment or rank units; an exponent between −0.25 and −0.75 to direct effort at the weakest domain while limiting false alarms; and not the minimum, which flags three quarters of adequate profiles as inadequate once measurement error is admitted.

articles.title: Simulation-based inference for cultural evolution: a tutorial with baby name data
articles.abstract: Cultural evolutionary models are usually easy to simulate but difficult to fit, because most have no tractable likelihood. Simulation-based inference (SBI) addresses this by treating the simulator itself as the likelihood, and now ranges from rejection-based approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) to amortized neural posterior estimation (NPE). Knowing which to use is hard, partly because they are rarely compared on the same model and data. In this tutorial I fit a Wright-Fisher-style model of baby name popularity to uncensored female naming records from South Australia (1944-2017, with inference on 1981-2017), comparing rejection ABC, ABC with random forests, and NPE with BayesFlow on one shared set of 10,000 simulations. The model includes frequency dependence (β), an age-dependent bias (α), and random variation (γ). Recovery varies widely across parameters and methods, from r = 0.96-1.00 for β to r = 0.39-0.97 for γ, and these differences track what each estimator does with the summary statistics it is given and, for γ, how much of the signal those statistics retain. I use the comparison to work through what makes a parameter identifiable, the diagnostics that indicate whether a posterior can be trusted, and common failure modes. All code and data are provided.

articles.title: Microdosing psychedelics: a case-study exploration of use modalities and the understanding and management of risk
articles.abstract: Background: In recent years, microdosing psychedelics has been a growing phenomenon attracting media, popular and scientific attention. The practice entails the use of sub-hallucinogenic doses of psychedelics substances such as LSD and psilocybin mushrooms. Users report a multiplicity of motivations for and benefits from engaging with microdosing that run across the enhancement/therapy continuum. At the same time, scientific research remains limited and inconclusive as to microdosing’s safety and effectiveness. Methods: The present paper draws on an extended, in-depth interview with a user of psychedelic microdosing to investigate key aspects pertaining to the practice. Results: The discussion focuses on the participant’s engagement with different substances, their understandings of the various risks potentially involved in microdosing, and how they manage these risks. Conclusion: The themes that emerge as significant out of these discussions relate to authenticity, identity and the broader dynamic and antagonisms between the world of psychedelics and dominant culture.

articles.title: Risk-Aware Infrastructure Forecasting for Early Childhood Capacity: A Hybrid Demographic-Housing Model with Algorithmic Governance
articles.abstract: This study presents a hybrid demographic-housing forecasting pipeline for preschool infrastructure demand in Singapore, designed for the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA). The model integrates cohort-component population aging with Build-To-Order (BTO) housing delivery signals and Census 2020 subzone-specific child-per-unit ratios, replacing fixed national coefficients that introduce up to 10% estimation error (Wilson et al., 2021). OLS regression models the population-to-child-count relationship (R^2=0.87), while Monte Carlo simulation (n=1,000) transforms deterministic point-estimates into probabilistic planning ranges, establishing a 95th percentile confidence bound recommending a three-center national safety buffer. The pipeline embeds algorithmic governance tripwires — automated buffer-consumption thresholds at 25%, 50%, and 100% — that mandate escalating executive intervention before fiscal floors are breached (NIST, 2023). A Social Return on Investment (SROI) reconciliation maps pedagogical outcomes across five weighted domains to the Heckman Equation, adopting a conservative 1.75x social return estimate (Heckman et al., 2010). Break-even analysis identifies a 3.5-month fiscal inflection point with a 4.62-month margin of safety for construction acceleration investments. Keywords: Infrastructure Planning, Early Childhood Education, Demographic Forecasting, Algorithmic Governance, Monte Carlo Simulation, Urban Analytics, Singapore Housing

articles.title: Productive Policy Competition and Asymmetric Extremism
articles.abstract: Viable policies must be developed by individuals and groups with the expertise and willingness to do so. We develop a model in which competing policy-motivated developers differ in their intrinsic ideological extremism and ability at crafting high quality policies. The unique equilibrium exhibits unequal participation, inefficiently unpredictable and extreme policies and outcomes, wasted effort, and an apparent advantage for extreme policies. While asymmetries between the developers always reduce observable competition, they can nevertheless benefit the decisionmaker. This contrasts starkly with the classic all-pay contest -- where the decisionmaker is always harmed by asymmetries due to the discouragement effect -- and results from the developers' policy motivations. I also introduce and solve a broader class of generalized policy contests that nests both the policy-development model and the all-pay contest, and develop new methods for solving asymmetric contests with spillovers. Broadly, my analysis provides a novel rationale for why extreme actors may dominate policymaking that is rooted in the nature of policy development, and highlights the difficulty in assessing the normative implications of such dominance.

articles.title: Violence and International Migration in Illiberal Times: The Case of El Salvador’s Authoritarian Transformation
articles.abstract: Across a new transnational wave of illiberal governance, tough-on-crime approaches to public safety and migration are growing. The case of El Salvador, in which President Nayib Bukele suspended due process protections and imprisoned suspected gang members in mass beginning in late March 2022 under a State of Exception policy, offers a window into this process. Turning to a combination of administrative datasets and cross-national surveys, we show that despite tremendous public approval for President Bukele’s strategies as the solution to a long history of persistent gang violence and international migration, violence largely reduced before he implemented the State of Exception, and Salvadorans’ migration intentions have not declined. Moreover, we find no evidence that the policy or Bukele taking office produced a particular reduction in Salvadoran migration to either the U.S. or Mexico compared to Guatemalan and Honduran migration. Nor do we uncover clear evidence that return migration to El Salvador uniquely increased, undercutting conclusions that illiberal tough-on-crime policies like El Salvador’s are likely to address “root causes” of international migration.

articles.title: The English Education System in the 16th- and 17th-centuries: Philanthropy and the Study of Science
articles.abstract: This article continues the topic of the reform of education in 17th-century England from the paper ‘Literacy and the education system in 16th- and 17th -century England’, published as preprint on this site in January 2026 (DOI: 10.31235/osf.io/zfs7r_v1). Gresham College and London as the 'third university' in England are the themes.

articles.title: The Non-Binarity of Artificial Intelligence Global Competition: 2018-2025
articles.authors: Wiebke Dorfs, Maximilian Hampel, Joanna J. Bryson

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Technological progress plays a crucial role in international relations. In particular, innovation has long been theorized as instrumental to power transitions. It is therefore unsurprising that the return of China as a global superpower and its technological advances has triggered considerable discussion. One narrative that has emerged is that of a binary "AI Cold War" competition between China and the US, similar to the 1947-1991 competition between nuclear superpowers. Another though is that the digital and information revolutions should facilitate technology and therefore power diffusion. Here we examine the claim of a binary competition, examining the state and trajectory of global AI competition for the years 2018, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. We use AI patents defended globally in the WIPO database and the market capitalization of the companies holding them as proxies for innovation and market power. We find that the binary narrative underestimates the strength of other actors globally, notably but not exclusively the European Union and Japan. These are comparable to China, and on the innovation metric with the US. In terms of market power, the US is a significant outlier, with an order of magnitude more capital concentration. Our research therefore indicates that any binary AI cold war narrative is not data-led.

articles.title: From Himalayan Catastrophe to National Resilience: Lessons from the 2026 Bhote Koshi and Trishuli River Floods in Nepal

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: The August 2026 Bhote Koshi–Trishuli disaster was not simply another flood. It was a cascading cryosphere disaster linking glacier instability, steep Himalayan topography, hydropower, highways, international trade, tourism, and pilgrimage—exposing weaknesses in transboundary observation, monitoring, and development planning (ICIMOD, 2026b; Reuters, 2026a). Nepal must treat it as a turning point. On the morning of 26 August 2026, the mountains above Nepal’s northern frontier delivered a disaster of almost unimaginable speed and scale. A massive mass of ice, rock, and sediment detached in the high Himalayan terrain near the Nepal–Tibet border, descended roughly 1,200 metres, interacted with the Lhende Khola system, and generated a debris-rich flood that surged through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors, destroying settlements, markets, roads, bridges, hydropower facilities, and an international border crossing and transforming them into fields of mud, boulders, and wreckage within minutes (ICIMOD, 2026b; Reuters, 2026a). Satellite analysis indicates that a substantial section of glacier and adjoining rock detached from approximately 5,200 metres elevation, while river levels downstream rose by as much as seven to nine metres within approximately half an hour in some locations (ICIMOD, 2026b; The Guardian, 2026). That rate left extraordinarily little time for people to recognize the danger, much less to evacuate. Although some areas were warned via police megaphones, announcements by the local governments, and mobile alerts, most people took it as regular seasonal flood warnings and missed the opportunity to escape.

articles.title: Religious Leaders and Distributive Politics in Postwar Italy
articles.abstract: How do unelected local leaders shape distributive politics? Religious authorities and other local leaders are often deeply embedded in the communities that receive public investment, yet many have no formal role in allocating or delivering state resources. I argue that such leaders can nonetheless shape distribution by increasing electoral returns to public investment. I test this argument using data on public works from a large-scale development program in postwar Southern Italy, exploiting variation in the election of Christian Democratic (DC) politicians and the local embeddedness of Catholic bishops. Difference-in-differences estimates show that DC politicians allocate more public works where bishops are locally embedded. These investments translate into higher DC vote shares specifically where bishops are local, with no evidence that bishops lobby for community- or Church-aligned projects or are rewarded for prior electoral support. These findings shed new light on the relationship between political intermediation and distributive politics.

articles.title: From Reach to Relationship: Reframing Social Media Recruitment as an Action Research Practice
articles.abstract: Social media is routine infrastructure for participant recruitment in health and social research, yet methodological discussions typically evaluate platforms by reach, cost, speed, targeting, and conversion. This paper reframes social media recruitment through an action-research lens, positioning recruitment as an early site where participation is constituted, relationships begin, power is negotiated, and learning occurs. Drawing on a critical integrative review of 22 empirical and methodological studies addressing Facebook/Meta, Instagram, X/Twitter, Reddit, WhatsApp, WeChat, and multiplatform recruitment, we examine the affordances and relational tensions of digitally mediated recruitment. Social media can reduce costs, accelerate access to dispersed and stigmatized populations, and enable iterative adaptation, but can also reproduce sampling inequalities, platform surveillance, algorithmic governance, hostile interactions, fraud, and verification labour. We introduce recruitment-as-inquiry: the proposition that recruitment helps constitute the participatory field rather than merely populate it. We propose six interconnected practices: co-defining recruitment purpose; selecting platforms with communities; treating invitations as relational encounters; reflexively examining participation, absence, and exclusion; protecting integrity without undermining trust; and returning recruitment learning to subsequent inquiry and action. This framework extends action research upstream, aligning digital recruitment with its democratic, relational, reflexive, and transformative commitments.

articles.title: Decreased Support for Political Violence in the United States in Mid-2026: Findings from a Nationally Representative Survey
articles.authors: Garen Wintemute, Sonia Robinson, Krista Neumann, Daniel Tancredi, Shaina Sta Cruz, Aaron Shev, Elizabeth A. Tomsich, Bradley Velasquez, Mona A. Wright, Veronica Pear
articles.abstract: Background: Recent survey research has found concerning but stable prevalences of support for and willingness to engage in political violence in the United States (US). This study re-estimates those prevalences in mid-2026—a midterm election year in which support for political violence might be expected to increase. Methods: Findings are from Wave 5, conducted May 15-June 15, 2026, of a nationally representative annual longitudinal survey of adult members of the Ipsos KnowledgePanel that was initiated in 2022. Primary findings are for the entire cohort; a secondary analysis examined responses by political party and Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement affiliations. Principal outcomes are measures of justification for, willingness to engage in, and anticipated firearm use in political violence. Results for individual years are presented as weighted prevalences and item scores. Change from mid-2025 to mid-2026 is estimated based on mean change scores. Results: The completion rate was 90.7%; there were 7,752 respondents. As in 2025, high levels of support for and willingness to participate in political violence were uncommon in 2026. Of 53 items addressing anticipation of, justification for, and willingness to commit political violence, 51 showed decreases from 2025 to 2026. All 51 decreases were small, but 35 were significant; only expectation of civil war increased significantly. Decreases from 2025-2026 occurred across the political spectrum. In 2026, MAGA Republicans and MAGA supporters who were non-Republicans were often more supportive of political violence than others, and the latter were often more willing to engage in it. Conclusions: Nearly all measures of support for and willingness to commit political violence decreased for the population as a whole, in many cases across the political spectrum. Higher levels of support for and willingness to participate in violence among MAGA supporters who were non-Republicans warrant further investigation. These findings can help advance prevention efforts, which are urgently needed in this US midterm election year.

articles.title: The Gender Pay Gap and the Child Tax Credit: Credit Eligibility and Unexplained Differences in Mothers’ and Fathers’ Earnings (Working Paper)

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: One of the most striking differences in eligibility for the full Child Tax Credit (CTC) is by family type (female and male heads of household and two-parent, married households). Differences in the wages of working mothers and fathers unexplained by key wage predictors can help explain these disparities. This paper explores the interactions between unexplained gender wage gaps and full CTC eligibility using data from the 2025 Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS-ASEC). We examine CTC eligibility across the earned income distribution by family type, estimate how much of the wage gap is unexplained by key wage predictors, simulate counterfactual wages and earnings for all working mothers absent this unexplained gap, and recalculate their families’ CTC. Findings suggest that unexplained differences in the wages of working mothers and fathers leave roughly 1.7 million mothers and 2.9 million children ineligible for the full CTC.

articles.title: Déchets solides ménagers du marché Nkoulouloun à Douala (Cameroun) : caractérisation, gestion et potentialités de valorisation dans une perspective d'économie circulaire
articles.abstract: Municipal solid waste management in urban markets is an environmental, economic and organizational challenge. This study analyses the characteristics of municipal solid waste generated at Nkoulouloun market in Douala II, its management practices and its valorisation potential within a circular economy perspective. A holistic-systemic approach was used, combining a literature review, direct non-participant observations, interviews with stakeholders involved in waste management and valorisation, and a questionnaire survey of 170 traders. Quantitative data were processed through frequencies and percentages using Excel and SPSS. According to data provided by the Douala II municipality, waste generation is estimated at about 50 tonnes per week. Organic waste accounts for 49.6%, plastics and textiles for 37.9%, and metals and other waste for 12.5%. Management involves collection and temporary storage by municipal sanitation staff, followed by evacuation by HYSACAM. However, 59.4% of surveyed traders reported evacuation after two weeks and 40% after three weeks. Nearly 80% reported declining sales associated with poor market sanitation; 66.4% reported damage to commercial property and 33.5% damage to merchandise. Interviews identified potential valorisation pathways for organic, plastic and metal waste, as well as stakeholders who could potentially be involved. The findings indicate that the composition of the waste stream offers valorisation opportunities, while implementation depends on source separation, collection, and infrastructure and stakeholder coordination. Keywords: municipal solid waste; urban market; circular economy; waste valorisation; waste management.

articles.title: Stockholm Syndrome: Origins, Evidence, and Institutional Legitimation
articles.abstract: This article examines whether Stockholm syndrome, a term that emerged from the 1973 Norrmalmstorg bank robbery, is supported by the available evidence. Using primary sources and a review of the literature, it finds that the psychiatrist who pioneered the label never assessed the hostages, that the hostages' behavior may reflect reasonable responses to danger, and that the term followed a hostage's public criticism of how police handled the situation. Drawing a distinction between the cultural reach of Stockholm syndrome and the clinical record behind it, the article explores the consequences of this gap for psychology and its neighboring fields. The term continues to appear in textbooks and applied settings despite this evidentiary gap. Scholarship also suggests that the label has often been applied along gendered lines, including to women whose responses were characterized as irrational. The term's wide circulation may have narrowed what questions get asked about captivity bonding and kept explanations like trauma bonding from receiving consideration. From this, the article develops a broader account it terms circular institutional legitimation, in which a construct gains apparent scientific authority through successive institutional adoptions that substitute for empirical validation.

articles.title: Political Coordination Without a Ruling Party: Informal Networks in Post-Revolutionary Iran
articles.abstract: The Islamic Republic of Iran dissolved its only ruling party in 1987 and has governed its provinces ever since without the organisation that comparative politics treats as essential to durable authoritarian rule. Yet elections have been held continuously, elites have circulated at extraordinary rates---roughly two in three parliamentary incumbents and four in five city councillors are replaced each cycle---and mass participation has persisted, with some 273,000 candidates registering for a single round of local elections. This article asks how political coordination is accomplished at the subnational level in the structural absence of party organisation. Drawing on original electoral data covering all eleven parliamentary terms and on remote qualitative fieldwork in Khuzestan Province, it argues that durable, territorially embedded informal networks---kinship and tribal structures, religious associations, patronage hierarchies, and economic coalitions---perform the coordinating functions normally attributed to ruling parties. Read through Gramsci's account of hegemony and the integral state, these networks constitute decentralised sites of consent production that complement, rather than replace, coercive and institutional power. The case of Dezful illustrates the mechanism. The argument specifies a model of network-based hegemony with implications for the study of authoritarian durability, party substitution, and informal institutions beyond Iran.

articles.title: Revisiting L1-L2 Processing Differences in NPI Licensing: A Maximal Mixed-Effects Approach
articles.abstract: This study reports a re-analysis of deMeurisse and Kaan's (2024) data on L1 transfer effects in negative polarity item (NPI) licensing, employing a maximal mixed-effects modeling framework. Whereas the original investigation relied on a reduced random-effects structure comprising only random intercepts by participants, we applied a more inclusive model that incorporates random slopes for licensing conditions by participants, following recommendations in the literature (Barr et al., 2013). A model comparison demonstrated that the maximal structure yielded a significantly superior fit (ΔAIC = 78.18), while the core L1 transfer effect remained stable under this more stringent analytical approach. These results reinforce the utility of maximal random-effects specifications in experimental psycholinguistics.

articles.title: Naming Violence: Obstetric Suffering, Emotional Communities, and Feminist Political Action in Spain
articles.abstract: This article examines how obstetric experiences came to be named and recognized as violencia obstétrica within the feminist association El Parto es Nuestro (EPEN) in Spain, and how that naming became the foundational act of a sustained political movement. Drawing on feminist ethnography conducted in Madrid between 2023 and 2024, including participant observation, twenty semi-structured interviews, and documentary analysis of the association's fifteen-year digital archive, I argue that naming is not merely descriptive but constitutive: it transforms isolated suffering into a shared grammar of pain, and that grammar becomes the infrastructure of collective feminist action. The article attends to three interrelated dimensions: the embodied transformation through which women move from self-blame to structural critique; the transnational genealogy of the category violencia obstétrica, which traveled from Venezuela and Latin America to Spain and thereby inverts conventional flows of feminist knowledge; and the internal fractures of the movement, which reveal that the emotional community built around obstetric violence is not homogeneous but shot through with inequalities of class, generation, religion, and race. Grounded in feminist anthropology, theories of epistemic injustice, and Myriam Jimeno's work on emotional communities, the article traces the trajectory from bodily dispossession to political subjecthood.

articles.title: Architectures of Denunciation: Feminist Infrastructural Labour, Digital Organising, and the Political Durability of Obstetric Violence
articles.abstract: This article examines how feminist digital infrastructures are organised, maintained, and made politically durable through the case of El Parto es Nuestro (EPEN), a Spanish association contesting obstetric violence. Drawing on feminist digital ethnography, including fourteen months of participant observation, twenty semi-structured interviews, 1,128 blog posts published between 2010 and 2024, the association's website, and seventeen campaigns, I ask how feminist organising becomes sedimented in digital architectures over time. I develop the concept architectures of denunciation to describe socio-technical arrangements through which dispersed experiences of harm are accumulated, classified, retrieved, connected to evidence, and made available for future mobilisation. The article argues that these architectures do not persist through technical affordances alone. Their political durability depends on feminist infrastructural labour: the often invisible work of tagging, maintaining links, preserving screenshots, translating, curating evidence, updating websites, and migrating archives. EPEN's trajectory shows that persistence is an organisational accomplishment rather than an inherent property of digital media. By bringing gendered affordances into dialogue with feminist organisation studies, I show how digital feminist activism is sustained through the interaction of socio-technical possibilities, collective maintenance, organisational memory, and finite volunteer labour. The article contributes to feminist studies of organising by demonstrating that infrastructures are not simply channels for activism but sites where feminist knowledge, memory, and political categories are continually reproduced.

articles.title: Changes in homeownership and entry into parenthood in the Nordic countries
articles.authors: INVEST Flagship, Jessica Nisén, Lars Dommermuth, Sofi Ohlsson-Wijk1, Peter Fallesen
articles.abstract: Since 2010, fertility levels have declined unexpectedly in all Nordic countries, with record lows being reached in recent years. The reasons for these declines are unclear, except that fewer people are becoming parents. The aim of this study was to investigate whether changes in housing tenure played a role in the declined entry into parenthood. We expected that changes in housing tenure, particularly a decline in homeownership related to housing affordability challenges among young adults, may have contributed to this decline. Using harmonized Nordic individual-level register data, we assessed to what extent changes in housing tenure, changes in fertility behavior within tenure groups, or both, contributed to the decline. Discrete-time event history models and multivariate decomposition were applied. According to our results, homeownership among young adults declined in the 2010s in Denmark and Finland – but not in Sweden or Norway. The decline in first births was only partially attributable to compositional change in housing tenure along with other socioeconomic factors in Denmark, Finland and Sweden. Entry into parenthood declined among women, regardless of their tenure status, in all four countries during the 2010s, suggesting the importance of behavioral changes. However, the decline was more pronounced among renters than homeowners.

articles.title: rcrisp: An R package for urban river space delineation
articles.abstract: rcrisp provides tools to automate the morphological delineation of riverside urban areas—i.e., the spaces surrounding a river where social, environmental and economic phenomena are assumed to be influenced by the presence of the river—following a method developed in Forgaci (2018, 88-89). The method is based on the premise that analyses of riverside urban phenomena are often done without a clear and consistent spatial definition of the area of interest and that a morphological delineation—combining the natural terrain of the river valley and the configuration of the overlapping built urban fabric—can provide a more objective and comparable approach. Delineations following this morphological delineation method enable integrated local analyses, where data from different sources must be combined within a neutral spatial unit, as well as global cross-case analyses, which require a spatial unit that is comparable across different geographic contexts. The method proposes a hierarchical delineation of four spatial units: the river valley, the river corridor, the corridor segments, and the river space (i.e., the area between the riverbanks and the first line of buildings). Accordingly, rcrisp includes functions to delineate each, as well as an all-in-one function that runs all desired delineations. The package also includes functions to download and preprocess OpenStreetMap (OSM) and global Digital Elevation Model (DEM) data, which are required as input data for the delineation process. The resulting delineations can be used in any downstream analysis of riverside urban areas that can benefit from consistent and comparable spatial units, including land use, accessibility, and ecosystem services assessments.

articles.title: Communication is not consultation: a documentary analysis of participation depth and the architecture of community engagement during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Introduction: Risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) is treated as essential to Ebola response, but routine reporting can collapse qualitatively different forms of participation into a single category of "engagement." We examined what kinds of participation were actually demonstrable in the documentary record of the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BDBV) response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and what the reporting system itself made visible. Methods: We conducted a documentary analysis of national outbreak SitReps and companion RCCE streams through 3 September 2026. A literature-informed 0--7 framework distinguished no documented interaction, information, sensitisation/mobilisation, feedback collection, consultation, negotiation, iterative participation, and co-design/shared decision-making. Exact source excerpts, actors, dates, sources and validation status were retained. The frozen primary dataset comprised 180 RCCE documentary units; 156 were validated directly to source PDF/text and physical page, and 24 late-window units were verified to the processed national stream pending original-page validation. Results: Thirty units (16.7%) were information, 111 (61.7%) sensitisation/mobilisation, 37 (20.6%) feedback collection, and two (1.1%) consultation. No source-verified unit demonstrated negotiation, iterative participation or co-design/shared decision authority. The response nevertheless possessed a substantial listening apparatus: community concerns included treatment-centre conditions, delayed safe and dignified burials, alert handling, decontamination, medicines, vaccines, clinical trials and body presentation. The documentary chain usually ended at feedback capture, clarification or exchange rather than a traceable decision-to-modification pathway. Conclusion: The 2026 response record documents extensive communication, mobilisation and social listening, but makes community influence over response decisions much less observable. The finding is not that deeper participation did not occur; it is that routine epidemic reporting was better equipped to demonstrate reach and feedback than negotiation, adaptation or shared authority. RCCE monitoring should therefore complement reach metrics with explicit feedback-uptake and decision-trace indicators. Keywords: Bundibugyo virus disease; Ebola; community engagement; participation; RCCE; co-production; social listening; documentary analysis; Democratic Republic of the Congo; epidemic governance

articles.title: The social production of epidemic data: response contestation, institutional disruption and surveillance observability during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo — a longitudinal documentary analysis
articles.abstract: Introduction: Epidemic surveillance is often represented as a technical pipeline converting cases, contacts, specimens and deaths into data. Sociology of quantification and Ebola social-science research suggest instead that the conditions for observation are socially and institutionally produced. We examine this during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Methods: We conducted longitudinal documentary analysis and within-case process tracing using Institut National de Santé Publique (INSP) situation reports and operational indicators. Candidate mentions were collapsed into unique episodes; event date was separated from report date; source labels such as 'resistance' were preserved but not treated as explanations; and core classification required a documented consequence for access, investigation, sampling, burial, screening, isolation or reporting. The analytic set was frozen at 1 September 2026; narrative streams were checked through 3 September for carry-forward and resolution. Results: Forty-six unique episodes were retained: 22 core observability events, 22 supporting disruptions without a demonstrated observation loss, and two ambiguous events. Observability was disrupted through heterogeneous mechanisms and actors, including armed-group and protest-related access constraints, community refusal, attacks on burial teams, provider strikes and non-payment, protocol refusal by humanitarian or military personnel, patient escapes, delayed team arrival, and security decisions releasing bodies before sampling. Several episodes documented repair after mediation, payment intervention or security support. Negative cases were informative: some attacks caused injury without a documented missed observation, and one multi-locality report recorded continued safe burials and swabbing despite source-labelled 'resistance'. Conclusion: Epidemic data are relational achievements. Missingness and delay can be endogenous to response relationships and institutions rather than merely technical defects. Treating heterogeneous mechanisms as generic 'community resistance' obscures both causation and correctable response failures. Surveillance systems should preserve structured metadata on non-observation, actor, mechanism and restoration to better distinguish absence of disease from absence of observation. Keywords: Bundibugyo virus disease; Ebola; epidemic intelligence; surveillance; observability; data production; community engagement; health systems; Democratic Republic of the Congo

articles.title: Refugee Return: Theory and Evidence
articles.authors: Ala Alrababah, Marine Casalis, Dominik Hangartner, Daniel Masterson, Jeremy Weinstein
articles.abstract: What explains refugee return? We theorize return as a two-stage process. Safety screens return, and other factors begin to shape who returns only after refugees judge it safe enough. We test this argument with an 11-wave panel of 3,003 Syrian refugee households in Lebanon from 2019 to 2026, spanning the fall of the Assad regime. Before the fall, the return rate averaged 1.6\% per wave despite worsening conditions in Lebanon, and baseline intentions rarely translated into return behavior. After the fall, the rate rose to 9.7\% per wave, while intentions, income, and networks became stronger predictors of return. Event-study estimates show that the increase was concentrated where the regime previously posed the threat: by the last wave, the return rate rose 10.1 percentage points (95\% CI [3.7, 16.5]) more in areas under the new government than under the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces. Qualitative interviews further show how safety shapes return.

articles.title: The Nexus of Voluntary Action and Humanitarian Imperative: A Comprehensive Analysis of Principled Service in Crisis Contexts
articles.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between voluntary action and humanitarian principles within contemporary crisis response frameworks. Drawing upon the foundational principles of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, particularly Voluntary Service, the analysis explores how volunteerism functions as both an ethical imperative and practical necessity in humanitarian action. Through documentary analysis and case study examination across five contexts—Lebanese Red Cross during civil war, Rohingya refugee camps in Bangladesh, youth volunteer exchange in Nepal, refugee volunteering in Uganda, and British Red Cross operations—the research investigates motivations, institutional frameworks, and impacts of voluntary humanitarian work. The paper argues that voluntary service constitutes an indispensable pillar of humanitarian response, yet faces increasing challenges including securitisation, resource constraints, and tensions between organisational principles and operational realities. The analysis reveals that while voluntary humanitarian action has evolved from wartime medical assistance to encompass comprehensive community resilience and development, its effectiveness remains contingent upon sustained institutional support, principled commitment, and recognition of volunteer agency. The paper concludes by identifying pathways for strengthening voluntary humanitarian action through enhanced partnership frameworks, sustainable funding mechanisms, and greater attention to volunteer wellbeing and motivation.

articles.title: “It’s a soul supplement”: an exploration of microdosing psychedelics through an in-depth interview with a user
articles.abstract: Microdosing consists of the regular use of sub-perceptive doses of psychedelics substances, most notably psilocybin (“magic”) mushrooms and lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD). First observed in specific environments and subcultures before spreading in wider areas of human activity, microdosing has become one of the better recognised faces of the current “psychedelics renaissance.” Building on a body of qualitative research that examines the reasons people engage with substance use, how their practice is embedded in the context of their everyday lives, and the ways these experiences shape them and are vested with meaning, this article draws on an extended, in-depth interview with a microdosing user. Approaching microdosing as a particular use modality of psychedelic substances, a number of interrelated issues are identified and explored in the discussion. These include the multiple, situated and shifting nature of motivations for microdosing, the gradual process of becoming entailed in the practice, the language and values used to express and signify the stance towards and experience of microdosing, the continuum of enhancement and therapy, and the two-way relationship between different use modalities (micro- and macro-dosing) undertaken by the same user.

articles.title: From Menarche to Motherhood: Fertility Patterns by Age at Menarche Across 40 Years in Norway
articles.authors: Kathryn Christine Beck, Øystein Kravdal, Maria Christine Magnus, Jonathan Wörn, Martin Flatø
articles.abstract: Age at menarche marks the onset of reproductive capacity, but its association with fertility has likely changed over time amid secular shifts in both menarcheal timing and fertility behavior. In this study, we examine how menarcheal timing is associated with first-birth timing, childlessness, and completed fertility across 40-years of birth cohorts in Norway using regional health survey data linked to administrative registers for over 60,000 women. Earlier age at menarche was associated with earlier entry into motherhood, although this association weakened in younger cohorts. By contrast, late menarche became increasingly associated with delayed first births and, in younger cohorts, with slightly lower completed fertility. These patterns were not explained by shared family background between siblings or by differences in educational trajectories between menarche groups. The findings suggest that developmental timing may play a larger role in explaining divergence in fertility outcomes, particularly with regards to the timing of childbearing, as family formation has shifted to later ages and life courses have become more individualized. These findings underscore how biological characteristics and social context jointly shape reproductive life courses and the importance of incorporating biological and developmental factors alongside social factors into demographic research on fertility change.

articles.title: Caste-based social exclusion and poverty in Nepal
articles.abstract: This study analyzes caste-based social exclusion and poverty using primary data collected from 448 households in Bheri municipality, Jajarkot district, Nepal, supplemented by secondary data from 34 companies listed on the Nepal Stock Exchange （NEPSE）. The collected data were analyzed using descriptive and econometric models such as the chi-square test, t-test, and binary logistic regression analysis. The study reveals that low-caste people are facing discrimination and social exclusion in accessing quality education and the labor market. These factors negatively affect their livelihoods, resulting in low-quality education, an income gap between upper and lower castes, and overall income inequality. These negative impacts contribute to consumption-based national poverty for low-caste and marginalized households in rural Nepal. Being low caste increases the probability of being poor by 1.533 times, which is statistically significant in less than 5%. Engagement in daily-based labor for their primary income sources will increase those households’ likelihood of being poor by 3.65 times compared to other sources of income, with a significance level of less than 1%. Moreover, having more dependent family members in households and engaging in subsistence farming also significantly contributes to falling into poverty. To enhance the livelihoods of low-caste and marginalized households, the government should prioritize combating poverty by increasing community engagement programs, ensuring equal access to the labor market, and quality education for these communities. Furthermore, private companies should also prioritize combating poverty through providing start-up business funds, job opportunity, and corporate social responsibility initiatives.

articles.title: Bridging Gender Gaps in Information Technology: Women’s Contribution to Economic Growth and Development
articles.abstract: The Information Technology (IT) sector has become one of the major contributors to economic growth, and women are playing an increasingly important role in its development. Women’s contributions have helped companies become more innovative, improve efficiency, and design products that meet the needs of a wider group of users. Hence, it is important to understand how the participation of women in the IT workforce influences innovation, productivity, employment, and overall economic performance. This review article discusses the growth of women's participation in technology, the challenges women continue to face, and the role of government initiatives and corporate policies in creating better opportunities. The study also explores the economic impact of women in the technology sector through case studies of Indra Nooyi, Susan Wojcicki, and Infosys, highlighting how leadership, innovation, and inclusive workplace practices contribute to business success and national development. The observations indicate that greater participation of women in the IT sector not only promotes gender equality but also strengthens innovation, expands employment opportunities, and supports sustainable economic growth. Continued investment in education, digital skills, and inclusive workplace policies will be essential for increasing women's contribution to the future digital economy.

articles.title: Urban Typology is not Destiny: The Succces of the High-Modernist Tower and Slab Public Housing as a Global Outlier in Singapore

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: In global urban discourse, the modernist tower-and-slab high-rise is almost universally pathologized as a spectacular failure of top-down social engineering. From Western public housing projects to post-communist concrete blocs, these monoliths are widely viewed as deterministic monuments to alienation and the limits of authoritarian high modernism. This paper challenges that architectural determinism by examining a stark global outlier: Singapore. In the city-state, high-modernist public housing not only survives but thrives, sheltering eighty percent of the population in highly livable, wealth-generating estates. By analyzing this spatial anomaly, this paper argues that the physical reality of the high-rise is not inherently criminogenic or socially isolating. The widespread global decay of this typology was fundamentally a downstream symptom of neoliberal abandonment and the hollowing of the welfare state. Singapore’s exception is sustained by fiercely guarded political-economic conditions: a radical state monopoly on land, the mobilization of captive domestic capital, and an ideological commitment to housing as a perpetual nation-building project. Ultimately, the Singaporean outlier proves that when insulated from market abandonment and continuously adapted to civic metis, the high-modernist high-rise ceases to be a dystopian relic, functioning instead as a highly livevable urban form.

articles.title: 22nd International Review of Leave Policies and Related Research 2026
articles.authors: Ivana Dobrotic, Ásdís Aðalbjörg Arnalds, Gayle Kaufman, Alison Koslowski, Peter Moss, Marie Valentova

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: The International Network on Leave Policies and Research has been producing an annual review of leave policies and related research since 2005 (for earlier reviews, go to the network’s website www.leavenetwork.org). The review covers Maternity, Paternity and Parental leaves; leave to care for sick children and other employment-related measures to support working parents; and early childhood education and care policy. The International Review is based on country notes from each participating country, prepared by members of the network and edited by a team of network members. Each country note follows a standard format: details of different types of leave; the relationship between leave policy and early childhood education and care policy; recent policy developments; information on take-up of leave. The International Review also includes definitions of the main types of leave policies; and cross-country comparisons. These comparative overviews cover: each main type of leave; the relationship between leave and ECEC entitlements; and policy changes and developments since the previous review. We also include a technical appendix. The 2026 International Review covers 53 countries. These are: Argentina, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Brazil, Canada, Chile, China, Costa Rica, Colombia, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Israel, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Korea, Kosovo, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Mexico, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Russian Federation, Serbia, Slovak Republic, Slovenia, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, United Kingdom, United States of America, Uruguay and Vietnam. Costa Rica is a new country note joining the review this year for the first time. The content of the International Review is to the best of our knowledge correct at the time of going to press, but mistakes may occur. If you should have a query or find an error, we would be grateful if you would contact the country note authors as relevant and the editors. We recommend that readers consult the most recent version of the International Review where possible, as we are unable to retrospectively rectify errors.

articles.title: Early Warning Signals of Sudden Changes in Walking Behavior
articles.authors: Dario Baretta, Alexandre Mazéas, Aïna Chalabaev, Jennifer Inauen, Guillaume Chevance
articles.abstract: Health-protecting behaviors such as walking are crucial for health, yet positive behavior changesare often accompanied by setbacks and relapses. Previous research suggests that critical fluctuations in behavioral time series might foreshadow relapses as early warning signals. This study examines the association between critical fluctuations, quantified as dynamic complexity(DC), and impending sudden changes in walking behavior. We analyzed step count data from 21,425 participants during enrollment in a digital physical activity intervention, covering a total of 5,474,501 person-days. Step counts were recorded via smartphones or wearables. Generalized multilevel models revealed a positive association between DC and impending sudden losses in walking (odds ratios [OR] 1.93 - 1.32). In contrast, the association between DC and impending sudden gains was weaker and less consistent (OR = 1.10 - 0.89). These findings provide evidence for the role of critical fluctuations as early warning signals for sudden losses in walking behaviorand highlight their potential in designing timely and targeted interventions.

articles.title: English-only publishing is a form of brain drain for non-English speaking countries
articles.abstract: By relying solely on English as science’s lingua franca, researchers are disconnecting them-selves from local knowledge systems, thereby diminishing their research impact on their societies and denying their local language the opportunity to grow its scientific lexicon. Over time, this ‘linguistic brain drain’ weakens local journals, marginalizes locally relevant research agendas, and deepens dependence on English-language publishers and indexers that privilege international visibility over local impact. Mitigation requires making modern science more inclusive. Specifically, promoting multilingual scholarly communication must be treated as development policy. Governments, universities, and funders should invest in local publishing infrastructures, reward multilingual outputs, support research addressing local priorities, and reform evaluation systems that undervalue non-English scholarship. Publishers and indexers should implement the UNESCO Recommendation on Open Science and the Helsinki Initiative on Multilingualism in Scholarly Communication. Generative AI, through the use of AI translators, can support multilingual scholarly communication. Challenges and their mitigations are further discussed.

articles.title: Weathering the Ballot Box: Climate Disasters Response and Electoral Behavior in Colombia

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Do voters hold politicians accountable for climate-related disasters? Existing research offers competing explanations: some argue that voters punish incumbents for poor disaster management, others emphasize the electoral rewards of effective relief, and still others highlight contextual conditions—such as disaster timing and intensity—that moderate these effects. This paper develops and tests a conditional accountability framework that integrates these perspectives, arguing that the political consequences of disasters depend jointly on disaster exposure and the credibility of government response. Using a novel dataset of over 47,000 climate-related disasters in Colombia (1998–2021), linked to municipality-level presidential election results, I estimate fixed-effects models capturing within-municipality and within-cycle variation in disaster exposure and relief. The results show that disasters generally reduce incumbent vote share when they are severe or occur close to elections, but that timely and visible relief can partially offset these effects. These findings unify competing theories of disaster politics and show how accountability under climate stress depends on the interaction between citizen evaluation and government strategy.

articles.title: Enhancing motivation through music therapy in subacute stroke rehabilitation: a within-subject crossover study
articles.authors: Theo Dimitriadis, Sjoerd Huisman, Mohammed Mudarris, Dieuwke S. Veldhuijzen, Andrea Evers, Wendy L. Magee, Rebecca Schaefer
articles.abstract: Objective This study examined motivation as a possible working mechanism for music therapy in stroke rehabilitation. We hypothesised that music therapy would lead to increased motivation for rehabilitation and explored its potential association with improvements in motor and/or functional and subjective (measures of) recovery. Methods Using a randomised within-subject crossover design, sixteen subacute stroke survivors received either Neurologic Music Therapy (NMT) plus standard care, followed by standard care only, or vice versa. The NMT intervention consisted of 6-9 half-hour sessions using Therapeutic Instrumental Music Practice and Music in Attention and Concentration Training. Motivation was assessed using the Brain Injury Rehabilitation Trust Motivation Questionnaire, alongside functional motor, cognitive, and quality of life measures. Results and Conclusions Music Therapy significantly increased motivation (p = .041), with an average increase of 8.72 in motivation scores during NMT plus standard care, while showing a 4.43 decrease during standard care alone. No significant association was found between motivation changes and cognitive or motor outcomes. Despite limitations due to missing data, the study suggests that NMT enhances motivation for rehabilitation in the subacute phase after stroke. Larger-scale studies are needed to evaluate the impact of music therapy-related increases in motivation on recovery.

articles.title: Recovering Collective Structure in Congressional Voting: A Fused Latent Factor and Network Approach
articles.abstract: Congressional voting reflects collective behavior structured by chamber-wide patterns such as partisanship and relational patterns among particular subsets of legislators, including factions and coalitions. Yet latent factor frameworks that dominate roll call analysis assume conditional independence across legislators and represent their ideal positions in a linear space. These restrictions can obscure relational patterns that do not align with chamber-wide latent dimensions. To model these behaviors, we adopt a fused latent factor and network model that captures chamber-wide patterns with the latent factors and attributes residual structure to the network. Applying this fused model to the 101st (1989--90) and 114th (2015--16) Senates, we first validate that the latent factors recover partisan voting patterns and identify two systematic failures of the latent factor: senators with moderate latent positions are assigned uncertain probabilities on party-line votes, and intra-party split votes exhibit systematic co-defection patterns. The network component closes the misprediction gap entirely for party-line votes but only partially for intra-party splits, capturing stable co-defection patterns while leaving more transient coalitions less predictable. Next, we apply a degree-corrected stochastic block model to the fitted network and recover interpretable voting blocs in both Senates. The 101st Senate features within-party factions that match historically documented coalitions and are driven by shared issue interests despite overlapping positions in the latent space. In the 114th Senate, the blocks take on an entirely different interpretation, uncovering two institutionally opposed coalitions: a cross-party governing bloc, including members of the Republican party leadership, and a Republican insurgent bloc, both driven by opposition of the other. Our findings demonstrate that roll call data alone contains recoverable signals of collective legislative behavior beyond partisanship that remain after accounting for chamber-wide partisan structure, and the organization of this collective behavior shifts from issue-based coalitions toward institutional conflict across decades of polarization.

articles.title: Towards a demographic analysis of kinship bereavement
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND Kin deaths are universal, but their frequency, timing, and position within family networks vary across demographic regimes. Existing demographic research describes kin loss, but provides limited tools for summarizing its cumulative and life-course consequences. OBJECTIVE We develop a demographic framework to compare bereavement regimes across populations, focusing on three dimensions: cumulative burden, loss of shared lifetime, and generational overlap in kin deaths.
