METHODS We derive three indicators from age-specific kinship dynamics: bereavement burden, defined from kin-years lived after kin death; shared time lost, measured as expected kin-years of potential coexistence removed by death; and generational overlap, measuring coincidence between age-specific death schedules of different kin types. We apply the framework to female 1950 cohorts in Argentina and Guatemala using UN-2024 data and matrix kinship models. RESULTS The comparison identifies contrasting bereavement regimes. Guatemala has much higher burdens from child and sibling deaths and larger total losses of shared time with these kin. Argentina has a higher grandparent burden and greater shared time lost per child death. Death schedules are also more strongly overlapped in Guatemala, particularly for siblings and parents and for children and parents, whereas Argentina displays a more sequential ordering of losses across generations. CONCLUSIONS Similar death counts can conceal markedly different bereavement experiences. The demographic meaning of loss depends on when deaths occur, how many kin are exposed, and how losses are sequenced across generations. CONTRIBUTION We extend formal kinship demography by providing three interpretable indicators that allow bereavement to be compared systematically across demographic regimes using standard population data.

articles.title: Does belief in supernatural punishment increase prosociality? Evidence from economic games in two religiously pluralistic communities of southern Benin
articles.authors: Augusto Dalla Ragione, Cody T. Ross, Marina Elodie Sedjro Djekinnou, Iranlowo Abakpin Elodie F Lawin, As'Ad Olawale Ichola Assani, Tossou Jeandro Simplice Kakpo, Daniel Major-Smith, Benjamin Grant Purzycki
articles.abstract: The role and durability of religious institutions in human societies has long been the subject of discussion among social scientists. A prominent view in anthropology considers religions-and especially moralistic religions-as institutions that enhance within-group cooperative proclivities and minimize norm violations, by inducing belief in the threat of supernatural punishment and monitoring. This may be particularly important in sustaining cooperation in larger groups, where mechanisms based on kinship, reciprocity, and reputation bookkeeping are less likely to be effective. The empirical literature is mixed, with some standardized cross-cultural studies providing support for claims of a relationship between moralistic punishment/monitoring beliefs and prosociality. For this study, we collected a suite of survey data on sociodemographics and religiosity, and ran economic experiments in two communities in southern Benin, West Africa. The communities are Vodun-majority, with an appreciable presence of Christians. This local religious diversity within the same ecological setting allows us to: (1) study the degree of syncretism between the two traditions, (2) evaluate whether Vodun and Christian believers attribute different levels of moralistic concerns to their respective deities, and (3) address the impact of belief in supernatural punishment on prosociality, as well as test for differences in effects between adherents of the two traditions. Our analyses reveal some statistically reliable associations between measures of religious cognition and experimental behavior, with increased perception of moralistic supernatural punishment being predictive of higher levels of prosociality. Our results, however, are sensitive to how religious cognition is measured, the type of prosocial behavior considered, and the specific religious community under study. We discuss our results within the framework of leading hypotheses on the nexus between religion and prosociality.

articles.title: As duas faces da classe no recrutamento político brasileiro
articles.abstract: Credential and wealth do not necessarily travel together, and they may operate at distinct phases of political recruitment. This article asks at which of them each one selects, entry into candidacy or the ballot box. The evidence is the universe of first-round candidacies registered with the Brazilian Superior Electoral Court between 1998 and 2024, 3.3 million records, whose occupation is turned into a continuous status score through the international classification of occupations, applied to this universe for the first time; occupation, schooling and declared assets for the same person meet from 2006 onwards. The two faces are compared with one another within each stage, never across stages. The correlation between occupational status and declared wealth is 0.195, and lower still among those elected. From the population to the pool of candidates the diploma already separates, by 0.34 of a standard deviation, whereas the ownership threshold does not; net of credential, entry runs mildly against the proprietor. At the ballot box the reading depends on the term of comparison, and against the mass of candidacies capital separates more than credential through owning any assets at all, while within the legal threshold, the minimum vote the law requires to take a seat, the distances shrink without the ordering between the faces changing, the diploma and the value of wealth tied at 0.103 and owning any assets above both, at 0.153. Office by office the faces run along distinct axes, credential following the federative hierarchy and capital the electoral formula, larger in majoritarian races. Class composition within each office barely moved over two decades, even as the share holding a degree nearly doubled. Gender is where the two faces stand furthest apart, because women arrive with more credential and less capital, and their schooling advantage reverses in general elections against the population of their own sex.

articles.title: Posting, Liking, and Messaging: The Correspondence Between Self-Reported and Actual Activities on Instagram and the Role of Question Framing
articles.authors: Frieder Rodewald, Florian Keusch, Szafran, Daria, Ruben Bach
articles.abstract: Research comparing self-reported and actual online behavior has focused primarily on general usage, such as how often individuals visit a platform or how much time they spend on it, and less on on-platform activities such as posting, commenting, or liking. We use respondents' actual behavior on Instagram, obtained through data donation, to examine how self-reports correspond to actual behavior, both for general usage frequency and for six on-platform activities. We test whether the direction of deviations between the two measures varies systematically with how often individuals actually use Instagram and how frequently they engage in each activity. We also test whether question framing affects correspondence for activities in a 2×2 survey experiment that varies the reference period (last seven days vs. typical week) and the response scale (numeric vs. vague quantifier labels). In a pre-registered study based on a probability-based online panel in Germany (n = 428 data donors), we find that self-reports of general usage frequency fall below actual usage for most respondents, and most so among frequent users. For on-platform activities, self-reports match actual behavior more often than they deviate from it, and the direction of deviations varies across activities. Higher actual engagement predicts underreporting for nearly all activities, whereas the association between lower engagement and overreporting is less stable. Contrary to expectations, the reference period does not improve correspondence for any activity, and numeric quantifier labels yield closer correspondence than vague quantifier labels for several activities. We discuss what these patterns imply for what self-reports and digital traces measure, and derive practical guidance for survey design in digital media research.

articles.title: The social structure of metacognition: the role of socioeconomic status and gender on students' self-assessment accuracy
articles.abstract: Educational inequalities are well documented, yet little is known about whether students’ ability to accurately evaluate their own academic performance is itself socially structured. This study examines socioeconomic and gender differences in metacognitive calibration – the alignment between students’ subjective assessments and objective performance – across compulsory schooling in Germany. Drawing on nationally representative data from the German National Educational Panel Study, we analyse mathematics and reading calibration from Grade 1 to Grade 9. Using fractional response models with flexible performance functions, we distinguish overall group differences in miscalibration from differences net of objective competence and examine how these patterns vary across the achievement distribution. Results show that objective competence is by far the strongest predictor of calibration: lower-performing students substantially overestimate their performance, and miscalibration declines with grade level. Raw socioeconomic differences in calibration are consistently observed, but they are largely explained by SES differences in objective achievement. Net SES differences are small and generally attenuate across grades, providing little evidence of an independent socioeconomic gradient in calibration. Gender differences follow a different pattern. In mathematics, girls are better calibrated than boys at comparable levels of competence, with the gap becoming larger in later grades and among higher-performing students. Reading differences are considerably smaller. These findings suggest that metacognitive calibration is strongly anchored in competence, while gendered patterns of self-evaluation may constitute a distinct dimension of educational inequality.

articles.title: For Whom Neighborhoods Matter in Early Childhood: Heterogeneous Effects on Achievement
articles.authors: Nicolai T. Borgen, Henrik Daae Zachrisson, Rosa Cheesman, Torkild Hovde Lyngstad, Eivind Ystrom
articles.abstract: The role of neighborhoods in shaping child and adolescent development is well-documented in empirical research. However, the extent to which neighborhood conditions differentially affect individuals based on their background and individual characteristics remains less explored, particularly during the first decade of life. This paper investigates the heterogeneous effects of neighborhood socioeconomic composition on academic achievement in middle childhood by combining Norwegian administrative data with genetic data from the Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Cohort Study (MoBa). Employing the Neighborhood Choice Model to address selection bias, we find that exposure to neighborhood disadvantage during a child's first ten years impacts 5th-grade standardized test scores. Furthermore, we find that the impact of neighborhoods varies considerably by socioeconomic background, gender, and children’s load for genetic variants correlated with educational attainment, estimated using within-family genetic variation. Notably, boys, children with a lower polygenic index for educational attainment, and those from families with lower incomes and parental education levels face the strongest neighborhood effects. Conversely, children with a higher polygenic index for education are unaffected by neighborhood disadvantage, as are children with affluent parents. These findings highlight the importance of studying heterogeneous neighborhood effects.

articles.title: What Instagram Records and What Users Report: A Data Donation Study Comparing Digital Traces with Self-Reported Behavior
articles.authors: Frieder Rodewald, Florian Keusch, Szafran, Daria, Ruben Bach
articles.abstract: Understanding how individuals use social media is central to research on its effects, yet most studies rely on self-reports. It remains unclear which behaviors platforms record at all, how closely self-reports correspond to those records, and how question design affects that correspondence. In a data donation study with a German probability-based online panel (N = 531 Instagram users, of whom 121 donated their data), we identified 93 digital traces available in Instagram's data download packages and extracted 49, spanning consumption, engagement, creation, and account management. Prevalence follows a steep gradient: consumption traces such as viewing are near-universal, engagement traces such as liking appear for a majority, creation traces such as posting appear for only a minority, and many specialized features are absent altogether, so several behaviors of potential interest can be studied only within the subgroup performing them. Self-reports correspond reasonably to actual behavior for deliberate, frequent behaviors (e.g., creating stories, liking posts), but poorly for passive consumption and rare behaviors. Experimentally varying the reference period and response format, we find significantly higher correlations under a typical-week framing for one behavior and no significant differences between response formats. We discuss when self-reports may suffice and when donated data is needed.

articles.title: The Dark Side of Legitimation. Experimental Evidence on the Effectiveness of Discursive Strategies Used by Cyber Criminals
articles.authors: Kristina S. Weißmüller, Tijs van den Broek, Alina Kaufmann, Steven James Watson
articles.abstract: Online, criminal organizations regularly use discursive legitimation strategies to influence public opinion about their criminal activities to justify their acts and minimize persecution. Yet, little is known about what types of strategies are effective in the case of criminal organizations. This study addresses this gap by identifying and quantifying how distinct discursive strategies impact citizens’ legitimacy judgment, their attribution of blame for societal harm associated with criminal activity and punitive intent. Using a discrete choice experiment conducted with representative citizen samples in Germany (n=301, Obs.=1,505) and the United Kingdom (n=350, Obs.=1,750), the study shows that distinct strategies can significantly impact citizens’ judgment about the legitimacy of criminal activity, their attribution of responsibility, accountability, and punitive intent. Cognitive and moral legitimation strategies – such as discrediting victims and legitimate institutions, but also signaling transparency and moralizing criminal action – are most effective. Social media amplifies, and higher societal harm reduces the influence of legitimation strategies. These novel insights advance the discourse on organizational legitimacy in the post-factual age of digital communication as well as scholarship on accountability and public opinion on criminal activity, helping practitioners and policy makers understand and counteract legitimation efforts by criminal organizations.

articles.title: Decentralization, Ethnic Fractionalization, and Public Services: Evidence from Kenyan Healthcare
articles.authors: Camille Hémet, Liam Wren-Lewis, Jessica Mahoney
articles.abstract: This paper examines the impact of ethnic fractionalization on public service use by exploiting a major constitutional reform in Kenya. Following an important period of inter-ethnic conflict, responsibility for local health services was decentralized to 47 newly created county governments. Using an event-study design, we find that use of public clinics for births increased significantly after the reform, but only in counties that were relatively ethnically homogeneous. We also find a significant increase in the correlation between county ethnic fractionalization and a range of other measures of public health service use. Services in these counties are also less likely to require payments after decentralization. Using within-county variation to investigate mechanisms, we find healthcare use increases were concentrated among areas and individuals of the same ethnicity as members of the new county government executives. Overall, the results suggest that more ethnically homogeneous sub-national jurisdictions can rapidly increase public service use.

articles.title: Four Kinds of Redundancy: Item Recoverability Across Five Survey Instruments
articles.abstract: Surveys often ask for more than they need to and some answers can be predicted from the other answers in the same questionnaire. This paper develops a measure for how much redundancy a questionnaire contains. Unlike work on shortening psychometric scales, the object here is the whole instrument including questions covering unrelated topics with no common construct. For each item, the measure asks how well that item can be predicted from the rest of the questionnaire, excluding the question block the items belongs to. Predictions come from cross-validated random forests. The measure is a simple skill score, R2 for continuous items and the Brier skill score for categorical ones. Both compare the model against a marginal baseline. This places items of different types, and questionnaires of different lengths, on one scale. The measure is computed from collected responses and requires data from a fielded sample. We apply the measure to five survey instruments. Looking at the most recoverable items shows that recoverability is not one phenomenon. It arises from different sources. It also reveals that few items could be dropped without losing information. The measure is therefore most useful as a diagnostic for questionnaire design.

articles.title: Sequential Structure Without a Linguistic Diagnosis: A Falsification-Oriented Analysis of the Indus Script
articles.abstract: The Indus Valley script remains undeciphered. Under ordinary cross-validated scoring, real Indus sign sequences show a positive trigram-over-bigram predictive gain (the two preceding signs predict the next sign better than one preceding sign alone), replicating closely across two independently extracted digitizations of the same underlying corpus tradition, including the M77 corpus corresponding to the concordance behind the most cited statistical studies of the script (+0.143 and +0.158 bits), and clearing 200-trial null distributions entirely. However, both corpora contain substantial exact-sequence repetition (23 to 33 percent of sequences). When cross-validation folds are constructed so duplicate sequences cannot appear in both training and their own held-out evaluation, the gain reverses sign for both corpora (-0.088, -0.083); when duplicates are instead collapsed to unique sequence types, it weakens to near zero (-0.023, -0.010). A control experiment, grouping sequences of the same size distribution but without duplicate identity, stays strongly positive, ruling out the alternative explanation that this reversal simply reflects smaller effective training sets rather than duplicate identity specifically. This is not a data-handling error, since the repetition is a genuine corpus property, but it means the ordinary-CV result should not be read as established evidence of sequential structure that generalizes to novel sequences, and we treat resolving this as the paper's central open problem. Independently of that question, our most specific test among the mechanisms we examined shows the ordinary-CV gain is not uniquely diagnostic of the particular linguistic generative mechanism we tested, including after rebuilding that generator and a non-linguistic alternative to match the real corpus's own vocabulary and length statistics; neither reproduces the real magnitude in matched or unmatched form. A sample-size curve on two calibration languages shows this estimator rarely returns a positive result below roughly 3,000 sequences for either, evidence against the ordinary-CV result being generic small-sample behavior. We also find evidence against inscriptions being deliberately constructed as globally unique identifiers, though not against more elaborate identifier schemes. The framework, derived corpora where licensing permits, and all experiments are released openly.

articles.title: Breaking the Glass Ceiling: Report on Understanding the Barriers Experienced by People of Colour Academics in the University Sector
articles.authors: Lutfun Nahar Lata, Sara Cheikh-Husain, Derlie Mateo-Babiano, Juliet Rogers, Yajie Li
articles.abstract: The report explores the experiences of racism faced by people of colour (PoC) academics at the University of Melbourne, the University of Sydney, and Charles Darwin University. Within and beyond academia, researchers have discussed how the legacies of colonialism and Eurocentrism continue to shape academic institutions and affect students and staff of colour in distinct ways. While universities are positioned as key actors in fostering inclusive societies, research consistently demonstrates that they also reproduce broader societal inequalities. Within this background, this research investigates the experiences of racism encountered by PoC academics at the University of Melbourne, University of Sydney, and Charles Darwin University. The findings reveal that racism permeates multiple levels of university governance and academic practices. Participants in this research highlighted issues such as the misrecognition and undervaluing of PoC academics’ expertise, institutional racism embedded in university policies and leadership, Eurocentric biases in curriculum, research, and organisational structures, exclusionary funding and publishing practices, and their university’s failure to address these barriers. They also pointed out Islamophobia, anti-Palestinian racism, institutional silence regarding these critical issues; professional isolation, limited professional networks, and disproportionate administrative burdens, particularly affecting migrant PoC academics.

articles.title: From Disaster to Resilience: Developing Smart Settlements in the Himalayas

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Nepal’s catastrophic 26 August 2026 Bhote Koshi–Trishuli flood should be understood not only as a humanitarian tragedy but also as a potentially major turning point in updating national settlement and reconstruction policy. Engineers and scientists have described the floods as a glacier–bedrock collapse that triggered an ice-rock avalanche and debris flow. As per the live updates on September 7, 2026, the total death toll was 1,355, and 4,996 people were missing (The Hindu, 2026). Indian and Nepali rescuers worked urgently to locate and rescue people buried under hydropower tunnels, buildings, mud, and landslide debris. UN News reported on September 3, 2026, that more than 22,000 children in the flood-affected region lacked safe drinking water (UN News, 2026). UNICEF also estimated that at least 19 schools had been damaged and that more than 10,000 school-age children urgently needed safe learning spaces (UN News, 2026). Coming just one year after the July 2025 flood in the same transboundary Lhende–Rasuwagadhi river system, this disaster underscores the risks of rebuilding vulnerable settlements and infrastructure in repeatedly exposed corridors. In the aftermath of this disaster, this article proposes Smart Settlement Guidelines for Nepal, informed by evidence on cryosphere-related hazards and disaster risks that resilient infrastructure, managed relocation, and disaster-resilient building practices can mitigate. Smart settlements should also account for Nepal’s remittance-dependent economy, local and imported food systems, and governance arrangements across local, provincial, and federal levels. Rather than advocating wholesale relocation of affected populations, the article advances a risk-differentiated approach: prohibiting new settlements in scientifically identified high-risk (red) zones, retrofitting viable communities, expanding river and slope buffers, and facilitating voluntary, rights-based relocation where residual risks remain unacceptable. Recognizing that disaster-related destruction does not extinguish property rights, relocation should be underpinned by fair compensation, land swaps, transferable development rights, and livelihood restoration.

articles.title: Emergence is not a phenomenon: Consilience as aspiration rather than metaphysic
articles.abstract: Scientists and philosophers invoke the term “emergence” to justify separations, or to stipulate relationships, between different human explanatory schemes, often held to constitute a hierarchy of scale or detail: physics, chemistry, biology, psychology, economics, sociology. Emergence is used to name or (allegedly) explain the inescapable experience that, though we believe bigger things are made of smaller ones, “higher-order” descriptions of larger things are often dramatically more effective than are attempts to reconstruct them from their constituent parts. This is often taken as a deep epistemological or ontological phenomenon or mystery. But this mystery appears only if we assume that one of our theories has already managed to fully capture the contours of some piece of reality. If we drop this assumption and view theories merely as limited and provisional toolkits for coping with different sorts of human problems, gulfs between paradigms cease to be ontological mysteries and become mere ignorance. The problem of emergence as a general phenomenon (rather than as a grab bag of specific puzzles about whether and how any theory can hook up to any others), can therefore be dissolved. This dissolution would help level out the hierarchy of the sciences and decrease epistemic hubris, with salutary implications for collective action and research strategy. We can still aspire to hook all our theories up with one another, but we need not assume that the world must go along with the attempt.

articles.title: Perceived Threats and Responses in AI Displacement Discourse: A Synthesis Literature Review on Student Susceptibility Through the EPPM Lens
articles.abstract: This literature review investigates how fear appeals related to artificial intelligence (AI) and job displacement are constructed in public discourse and how these narratives may influence students’ perceptions of academic and career security. Guided by the Extended Parallel Process Model (EPPM), the review synthesizes findings from discourse analyses, media framing studies, and student-focused research. The analysis reveals that severity framing is common in portraying AI as a threat to employment, while susceptibility framing, though less explicit, emerges particularly among students and early-career individuals. Coping appraisal outcomes vary, with some discourse encouraging upskilling (danger control), while others evoke resignation and anxiety (fear control), especially where perceived self-efficacy is low. The findings highlight a disconnect between public narratives and the actionable guidance needed to foster adaptive responses among students. The review concludes by discussing implications for education, communication, and future research on fear appeals in the context of AI-driven technological change. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Fear Appeals, EPPM, Job Displacement, Student Anxiety, Media Framing

articles.title: “An accompanied abortion is a safe abortion”: Organizational transformations in feminist abortion accompaniment across Latin America
articles.abstract: Over the past decade, feminist abortion accompaniment in Latin America has expanded and diversified, encompassing safe-abortion information hotlines, territorially rooted accompaniment groups, digital forms of support, and regional networks. This article examines these organizational transformations and the ways feminist organizations produce, systematize, and circulate practical abortion knowledge across different legal and institutional contexts. Drawing on nine interviews with activists in Argentina, Chile, Peru, Venezuela, and Colombia, together with organizational documents and field materials accumulated through previous research, the analysis approaches accompaniment as a heterogeneous organizational field rather than a single regional trajectory. The findings show that accompaniment has become a site of collective knowledge production through training, popular-education spaces, protocols, manuals, documentation, and data systematization. Second-trimester accompaniment makes this process particularly visible, showing how experience from individual cases can be collectively discussed, adjusted, and transformed into shared organizational knowledge. The persistence of feminist accompaniment after abortion legalization in Argentina further demonstrates that legal access does not render activist support obsolete. I conceptualize these processes as feminist pedagogies of care, referring to the organizational practices through which situated knowledge is taught, debated, systematized, and circulated while remaining embedded in relations of care. Regional articulations facilitate this circulation without producing a single model, making knowledge transferable while preserving local adaptation.

articles.title: Pride and Performance: Investigating Self-Presentation in Admiration Narratives through the Lens of Narcissism
articles.authors: Emmi Koskinen, Pentti Henttonen, Matias Piispanen, Liisa Voutilainen, Mariel Wuolio, Anssi Peräkylä
articles.abstract: This article explores how individuals narrate experiences of being admired and how these narratives reflect different self-presentation strategies. We utilized conversation-analytically informed narrative analysis to study 22 Finnish dyadic conversations, where participants told each other about their experiences of admiration. To increase the variability in the produced narratives, the dyads were composed of participants who exhibited either high or low levels of grandiose narcissistic traits. Three narrative orientations emerged: downgraded tellings, which minimize admiration; achievement-oriented tellings, which link admiration to specific actions; and hubristic tellings, which present admiration as enduring and tied to personal qualities. The findings illuminate how self-conscious emotions and personality traits can shape impression management in everyday talk. The results are interpreted through the theoretical lens of Cooley as well as Goffman’s framework concerning self-presentation in social interaction. We end the paper with the hypothesis that narcissistic participants utilize more competitive and self-enhancing strategies over minimizing approaches.

articles.title: Do Voters Blame the Opposition for Losing in Electoral Autocracies? Evidence from Turkey
articles.abstract: How do voters in autocracies evaluate opposition performance after defeat? We study this question with an exploratory online survey of 1054 opposition voters six months after Turkey's 2023 presidential and parliamentary elections. Although the opposition operated under structural disadvantages typical of electoral autocracies, nearly two-thirds of opposition voters blamed the opposition for the loss. Open-ended responses reveal three sources of dissatisfaction: criticism of the presidential candidate, frustration with intra-coalition conflict, and discomfort with the ideological breadth of the alliance. While these concerns often reflected genuine weaknesses in the opposition campaign, several were also intertwined with constraints imposed by the authoritarian context. To capture this tension, we introduce the concept of the authoritarian double bind: opposition parties are constrained by the regime in ways that produce the very weaknesses for which voters hold them accountable. Our findings show how electoral autocracies can simultaneously constrain opposition performance while voters continue to hold the opposition accountable for electoral failure.

articles.title: The Internal Logic of Professionalism: Reclaiming Emotional Engagement and the Limits of Standardised Care
articles.abstract: This paper argues that emotional engagement is not a discretionary adjunct to clinical practice but a constitutive element of the internal logic of professionalism. By tracing healthcare’s movement from professional deference to the metrified surveillance of the audit society, this paper examines tensions between threshold competence, person-centred care and professional discretion. Drawing on Nguyen’s (2021) critique of transparency, it argues that the standardisation of care virtues may encourage value capture and justificatory paranoia, potentially contributing to defensive emotional retreat. Patients’ intimate reasons may be difficult to express fully through auditable metrics without loss of context and meaning. Yet this epistemic limit does not entail secrecy or exemption from accountability. On this basis, the paper proposes that clinical opacity be understood as bounded protection for tacit and relational judgement, accompanied by proportionate review and institutional compassion. The paper therefore proposes a coherent moral settlement in which threshold competence, reflective engagement, emotional engagement and context-sensitive practical wisdom (phronesis) jointly support person-centred care.

articles.title: The (Liberal) Democratic Challenge of Public Administration

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Debates on democratic backsliding have prompted public administration scholars, notably Kutsal Yesilkagit and Michael Bauer, to argue that administrations facing illiberal populism must abandon neutrality and actively resist — even against electoral majorities. This paper examines Bauer's recent attempt to ground such resistance in Hegel's philosophy of right, which recasts bureaucracy as an ethical mediator embodying practical reason rather than a mere instrument of political rule. Through a close reading of Hegel's original text, this paper argues that Bauer's Hegelian turn imports more than a theory of administrative ethics: it imports Hegel's broader project of a "sovereignty of reason" directed against arbitrariness in politics as such, not merely against its populist variant. Read against contemporary diagnoses that locate liberalism's crisis in excessive depoliticization rather than its absence, this suggests that Bauer's strategy risks reinforcing the very populist grievances it seeks to counter. The paper concludes by outlining the need for a normative foundation of public administration that supports a politics of freedom without positioning itself against politics itself.

articles.title: Why Classroom Composition Matters: Relative Standing, Peer Exposure, and Educational Inequality
articles.abstract: Why has peer achievement research produced positive, null, and negative effects? We argue that the composition of classroom achievement combines two distinct pro- cesses. Higher-achieving classmates can improve the learning environment through knowledge, behaviors, and academic norms, but they also alter students’ relative standing within the local achievement hierarchy. Conventional peer-effect estimates may therefore combine learning and positional effects that operate differently across students. We examine these processes using longitudinal administrative data from Italy, following students from Grade 5 to Grade 8. To separate peer characteristics from prior joint exposure, we measure the Grade 5 achievement of newly encountered Grade 8 classmates. We assess within-school classroom sorting using a permutation- based diagnostic and exploit within-student, across-subject variation between Italian and Mathematics. This design compares the same student with the same classmates across subject-specific achievement environments while accounting for own prior achievement. Both peer achievement and relative standing are positively associated with subsequent achievement when modeled jointly, but the positional association is substantially larger. These relationships are also strongly heterogeneous. Learn- ing effects become more favorable as prior achievement increases, while positional effects are particularly pronounced among high achievers; their joint pattern also varies by socioeconomic background. The results recast classrooms as both learning and positional environments and show why average peer effects can obscure how classroom composition shapes achievement

articles.title: Street Takeovers and Youth Public Gatherings: An Analytical Distinction
articles.abstract: Street takeovers — events in which participants use motor vehicles to perform stunts on public roadways — and youth public gatherings — large informal assemblies of young people in public space for the purpose of collective social presence — are distinct social phenomena that have been consistently conflated under the label “teen takeover” in media coverage, policy discourse, and institutional response. This analytical note, grounded in content analysis of publicly available media documentation and informed by the author’s research-grounded working definition of youth public gatherings, establishes the analytical distinction between these phenomena along six dimensions: the role of the vehicle, the relationship to public space, formation and organization, participant demographics and racial and gendered dynamics, the risk profile, and the nature of filming and documentation. The note argues that this conflation shows how the label “teen takeover” operates — encoding a verdict of threat before evidence is examined and foreclosing the distinctions that would allow appropriate, differentiated institutional responses. Establishing this distinction is the analytical foundation for understanding each phenomenon on its own terms.

articles.title: Protected Bike Lanes Are Not Created Equal: A Review of Design, Safety, and Mobility Outcomes
articles.authors: Sudhir Bharati, Prabesh Kafle, Stuti Khatiwada

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Objectives: This study synthesizes current evidence on protected bike lane design to examine how design characteristics influence cyclist safety, mobility, and unintended consequences. The review evaluates whether facility performance varies according to separation type, directionality, buffer width, intersection treatment, and roadway context. Methods: A structured narrative literature review was conducted using Google Scholar to identify relevant studies published through March–April 2026. 150 publications were screened, and 66 studies were included following title, abstract, and full-text review. Findings: The reviewed literature shows that protected bike lanes improve cyclist safety and encourage cycling. These benefits depend on design quality rather than the simple presence of physical separation. Facilities with continuous physical separation, adequate buffers, and well designed intersection treatments yielded the greatest safety benefits. Interrupted protection and poorly managed conflict points reduced effectiveness. Protected facilities produced larger increases in cycling than conventional bike lanes, particularly within connected, low stress networks. Reported unintended consequences such as congestion, business impacts, and public opposition were generally smaller than commonly perceived. These issues were more often associated with implementation and operational challenges rather than the infrastructure itself. Novelty: Unlike previous reviews that primarily compare protected and conventional bicycle facilities, this review synthesizes evidence across safety, mobility, and implementation outcomes to demonstrate that protected bike lanes should be evaluated according to specific design characteristics rather than as a single infrastructure category. Practical Applications: The review provides evidence-based guidance for transportation agencies by identifying design features that consistently improve performance and highlighting the importance of context-sensitive planning, intersection design, network connectivity, and standardized post-implementation evaluation to support future bicycle infrastructure investments.

articles.title: StreetOps: An Open Computational Framework for Integrating Street Networks and Urban Operations into Adaptive Urban Design
articles.abstract: Urban planning has developed a rich computational ecosystem for acquiring spatial data, representing street networks, analyzing movement, modeling travel demand, measuring accessibility, and simulating transportation systems. Yet these tools generally terminate at description, diagnosis, or simulation. The final movement from observed urban operations to physical, regulatory, and programmatic design remains largely ad hoc, difficult to reproduce, and dependent on expert interpretation that is rarely encoded or reported. This article proposes StreetOps, an open computational framework for translating urban operations into design. StreetOps is conceived as a compositional layer built on existing open-source geospatial tools and standards rather than as a replacement for them. Its central technical abstraction, the OpsGraph, represents infrastructure, activities, temporal conditions, operating rules, public priorities, conflicts, and candidate interventions within a common time-aware and rule-aware model. The framework organizes analysis into six stages: acquire, integrate, diagnose, translate, generate scenarios, and evaluate. A proof-of-concept application to autonomous-vehicle pick-up and drop-off activity in Hayes Valley, San Francisco, illustrates how spatial and temporal sorting can be converted into targeted, adaptive curb-design responses while protecting transit, accessibility, pedestrian safety, and other public functions. The article defines the research problem, data model, translation logic, software architecture, governance principles, and development roadmap for StreetOps. Its intended contribution is to make the evidence-to-intervention step of urban planning more explicit, auditable, reusable, and reproducible.

articles.title: The Heterogeneous Effects of Data Transfer Restrictions on Data Centre Geography
articles.abstract: Restrictions on cross-border transfers of personal data are a non-tariff barrier to trade in data-processing services. We study whether the barrier moves computation onshore, and in which countries. We combine a country–year panel of data-centre openings in 158 countries with a new classification of national transfer regimes, and estimate event studies around the first adoption of GDPR-level rules. The response concentrates where compliance- exposed market size is large: openings rise 49% above the pre-treatment mean in downstream economies and 32% in high-GDP economies; the unconditional average is only weakly pos- itive and imprecise. Crypto data centres, which fall outside personal-data law, do not respond. We develop a compliance-quota model of investment location, in which tightening can reduce total compute while raising domestic data-centre investment.

articles.title: (FULL GUIDE) A Guide for Social Science Journal Editors on Easing into Open Science
articles.authors: Priya Silverstein, Colin Elman, Amanda Montoya, Barbara McGillivray, Charlotte Rebecca Pennington, Chase H. Harrison, Crystal N. Steltenpohl, Jan Philipp Röer, Katherine S. Corker, Lisa M Charron
articles.abstract: Journal editors have a large amount of power to advance open science in their respective fields by incentivising and mandating open policies and practices at their journals. The Data PASS Journal Editors Discussion Interface (JEDI, an online community for social science journal editors: www.dpjedi.org) has collated several resources on open science in journal editing (www.dpjedi.org/resources). However, it can be overwhelming as a new editor to know where to start. For this reason, we have created a guide for journal editors on how to get started with open science. The guide outlines steps that editors can take to implement open policies and practices at their journal, and goes through the what, why, how, and worries of each policy/practice.

articles.title: Moving academia towards its safe and just space: reflections on activating scientists
articles.abstract: Universities have immense potential to lead transformative climate action, yet they are largely failing to do so. We previously identified academic culture, with its focus on commercialisation, metrics, and competitiveness, as impediments to academic climate action. Building on Kate Raworth’s Doughnut Economics framework, we proposed an alternative vision, Doughnut Academia, which offers lessons for staying within human and planetary boundaries (Urai & Kelly, 2023) and issues a call to action that starts with culture change in scientific communities. In this essay, we reflect on the process of developing a participatory Doughnut Academia workshop, which aims to catalyze culture change and encourage people to find their own ways of engagement. Participants report that the workshop had multiple positive and enabling impacts on their research, teaching, institutional advocacy, activism and science communication. To encourage independent dissemination and wider engagement, we provide materials and advice for hosting the workshop. Finally, we reflect on the value of bottom-up approaches, such as our workshop, for bringing colleagues from all disciplines into dialogue about climate action.

articles.title: Dynamic Social Vulnerability Index (DSVI): A Mobility-Adjusted Measure of Community Vulnerability
articles.authors: Owais Gilani, Elena Khusainova, Talha Ali, Abby Flynt, Paul Christine, Simon Urbanek, Michael J. Kane
articles.abstract: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) serves as a useful tool to identify vulnerable communities in order to meet their needs before, during, and after disasters, infectious disease outbreaks, and other public health emergencies. Additionally, the SVI is widely used in social science research as a proxy measure of social disparities and as a measure of a community’s social determinants of health. We argue that social vulnerability, assessed in terms of a community’s access to different resources, is not solely determined by residential location but also by the locations that its residents frequent throughout the day, as determined by their movement. Building on the concept of activity spaces for individuals, we propose the idea of an ``activity space for communities'', which is an aggregate measure of the activity space of all individuals who consider that community their ``home''. In aggregate, residents of different communities will tend to have very different movement patterns, and hence different activity spaces. Using large-scale cell-phone telemetry data for the United States in 2019, we quantify this activity space for communities at the census tract level and apply it to SVI to develop a mobility adjusted measure of community vulnerability - the Dynamic SVI (DSVI). By incorporating mobility patterns into SVI, we move toward a relational and dynamic model of vulnerability, where risk is understood not just as a product of fixed geographic location, but also as shaped by daily movements, access to transportation, and the spatial distribution of critical resources and services. A web application to explore and download the DSVI for 2019 is available at https://mobility.science/dsvi.

articles.title: THE MEDIATING ROLE OF BUDGET RATCHETING ON OWN-SOURCE REVENUE AND REVENUE SHARING FUNDS' EFFECT ON CAPITAL EXPENDITURE
articles.authors: Faisal, Akmal Huda Nasution, Edy Zulfiar, Mariana, Anhar Firdaus, Rulyanti Susi Wardhani
articles.abstract: Objectives: This study aims to analyze the direct effect of Local Own-Source Revenue (PAD) and Revenue Sharing Fund (DBH) on Capital Expenditure, as well as to examine the mediating role of Budget Ratcheting in these relationships. Methodology: The research employs a quantitative approach with multiple linear regression analysis, utilizing time-series cross-sectional data from 23 regencies/cities in Aceh Province over a five-year period (2018–2022). Data were obtained from audited Local Government Financial Statements (LKPD), covering PAD, DBH, Capital Expenditure, and Budget Ratcheting variables. The analysis was conducted using SPSS version 25, with classical assumption tests applied to ensure model validity. Findings: The results show that PAD does not have a statistically significant effect on Capital Expenditure (p = 0.234), suggesting the presence of contextual influences such as governance quality and fiscal policy implementation. Conversely, DBH demonstrates a significant positive impact on Capital Expenditure (p = 0.000), consistent with prior studies emphasizing its role in enhancing local government investment capacity. Mediation analysis reveals that Budget Ratcheting strengthens the relationship between PAD and Capital Expenditure despite the initial insignificance (p = 0.015). Moreover, Budget Ratcheting mediates the relationship between DBH and Capital Expenditure with a notable negative adjustment effect (p = 0.005). Conclusion: The study highlights the critical role of revenue-sharing mechanisms and adaptive budgeting practices in supporting regional development. Strengthening fiscal management and enhancing budget flexibility are recommended strategies to maximize the effectiveness of local revenue streams in driving capital expenditures.

articles.title: Typology-based optimization reveals urban stream restoration priorities for biodiversity, climate adaptation and quality of life
articles.authors: Yehan Wu, Claudiu Forgaci, Nora Franzke, Ulrike Haase, Henriette John, Karol Dawid Mrozik, Ralf-Uwe Syrbe
articles.abstract: Urban streams are expected to support biodiversity, climate adaptation and quality of life, yet restoration priorities are difficult to compare across networks. We analyzed 4,668 100-m stream segments across four Central European cities using a cross-case typology and Pareto optimization, identifying four corridor types: Urbanized high-pressure, Open low-access, Riparian-rich green and Steep valley. No type performed best across all goals. Optimal interventions differed by type: reducing impervious cover in Urbanized high-pressure corridors, reducing edge density in Open low-access corridors, combining lower edge density with longer slow-mobility routes in Riparian-rich green corridors, and increasing riparian tree cover in Steep valley corridors. For each corridor type, prioritized strategies involving only one or two interventions predicted increases of up to 18.8% in biodiversity, 12.5% in climate adaptation and 19.9% in quality of life. Increasing open space cover was absent from all optimized strategies, and adding interventions did not consistently improve all three goals. These findings show that urban stream restoration has no single best solution: priorities need to match corridor conditions while balancing ecological, climate and social goals across the whole stream network.

articles.title: When Aging No Longer Means Turning Right: Evidence from Swiss Panel Data
articles.authors: Lena Ajdacic, Matthias Enggist, Reto Mitteregger
articles.abstract: By adopting a generational lens, research has increasingly documented political and electoral transformations in Western Europe. In parallel, many researchers have pointed to the crucial relevance of the formative years to understand attitudinal development. However, these approaches often dismiss that generations’ formative years can differ, with newer generations marrying later, having fewer children, and completing education later in life. Using data from the Swiss Household Panel (1999-2022), we analyze whether different generations in Switzerland show diverging age effects regarding political ideology. Find-ings from an interaction analysis of age and cohort show that while previous generations consistently tended to become more right-wing as they aged, members of Generations Y and Z remain largely stable in their ideological orientation over the life course. We find that this pattern is not explained by changes in demographic and socio-economic compo-sition between cohorts. The results of this study not only have important implications for future studies analyzing age-period-cohort effects, but also enhance our understanding of opinion formation in transforming postindustrial societies.

articles.title: From Networks to Mission Platforms: A Graded Architecture for Interdisciplinary Research at Institutional Scale
articles.authors: Jesus Marco de Lucas, Victoria Moreno-Arribas

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Large multidisciplinary research organisations face a well-documented tension: their breadth is precisely what makes them suited to complex societal challenges, yet their disciplinary structure (centres, areas, evaluation panels) makes interdisciplinary work costly to initiate and hard to sustain. This paper presents a longitudinal institutional case study of the approach adopted by the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) — Spain’s largest public research organisation, with more than 1,500 research groups in around 120 institutes — to address that tension without restructuring the institution. From 2018 onward CSIC developed a graded set of three collaboration instruments: Conexiones (light, bottom-up thematic networks), Interdisciplinary Thematic Platforms (PTI: mission- oriented, three-year, challenge-driven platforms with an ESFRI-derived design questionnaire) and Extended Platforms (PTI+: large-scale platforms with a four-line work structure, a consortium- agreement style governance and centralised financial management, created to absorb investments above C10M). The design principles of each instrument, the formal texts that implemented them and the governance rules are presented (dual coordination across centres, assembly/executive-committee model, two-thirds quorum, individual veto, VICYT ratification, Team Science and Open Science recommendations). Publicly available documentary evidence on outcomes up to 31 August 2026 is then compiled for the best-documented platforms and networks, including the PTI Salud Global response to COVID-19, the QTEP quantum ecosystem, SusPlast pilot plants, the IPCC Interactive Atlas delivered under PTI Clima, the Conexiones cohorts created in 2023 and 2025, and the 2026 migration of the Teledetect remote-sensing platform into the EarthWatchHub Conexión. The documentary record supports four observations: (i) a pre-existing platform template enabled unusually rapid institutional mobilisation during COVID-19; (ii) the platform architecture and its core governance principles were adapted to an increase of roughly two orders of magnitude in financial scale; (iii) a graded portfolio allowed organisational migration between instruments instead of simple termination; and (iv) different instruments generated documented joint activities and outputs. The instruments were subsequently formalised, not discontinued, by the administration that succeeded the one that created them. A set of transferable design propositions is derived from the case, and the limitations of a documentary analysis without a counterfactual are discussed. The contribution is a longitudinal institutional case showing how a large disciplinary research organisation can superimpose a graded set of transverse collaboration structures on its existing organisational backbone without dismantling it.

articles.title: Inhabiting a flammable landscape: wildfire, human (im)mobility, and the ambivalent role of neo-rural settlers in central Portugal.
articles.abstract: Wildfires are increasingly reshaping human mobility. Yet research treats the relationship as one-directional — mobility as an outcome of fire, or as its precursor — and looks mainly to North America and Australia. The depopulating interior of Southern Europe, where the fire regime is itself a product of past rural out-migration, has drawn far less attention. Drawing on immersive fieldwork and 25 semi-structured interviews conducted in 2024 in the Serra do Açor, central Portugal, seven years after the 2017 fires, I examine how wildfire and human mobility co-constitute one another, and find them bound recursively rather than causally. The fires did not deter in-migration but appear to have lowered barriers to it, while driving a slower out-migration among traumatised newcomers and owners of unrebuilt second homes. Place attachment and voluntary (im)mobility sustain an explicit, locally transmitted doctrine of staying to defend, even as the year-round settlement of isolated quintas (dispersed smallholdings) by newcomers inverts a historical logic and produces new spatial vulnerability alongside dense grassroots adaptation. Neo-rural settlers thus emerge as agents of vulnerability and of adaptation at once, and repopulation is best understood not as the reversal of a depopulation-driven fire regime but as its next chapter.

articles.title: Does Sports Betting Satisfy the Conventional Investment Criteria? Evidence from Administrative and Socio-economic Data from Tanzania
articles.abstract: Sports betting has become one of the fastest-growing sectors in Tanzania, generating substantial tax revenues and attracting greater participation, particularly among youth population already facing the unemployment crisis. Meanwhile, betting is increasingly regarded by many young people as a legitimate investment platform rather than entertainment, as is commonly the case. This study examines whether betting satisfies the core characteristics of investment and assesses associated risks using Tanzania-specific evidence. The study applies administrative data from the Gaming Board of Tanzania (GBT) and secondary data on youth employment from NBS. Using an investment assessment framework based on value creation, expected returns, and investor control, the study evaluates betting against established investment principles. The findings indicate that betting does not satisfy conventional investment criteria. Unlike productive investments, betting does not create underlying economic value, offers negative expected returns for most participants, and provides limited control over outcomes. The findings further suggest that betting functions primarily as entertainment and, for some young people, as a perceived response to economic uncertainty rather than a viable investment strategy. The paper recommends strengthening financial literacy programs, discouraging more participation via taxation, improving consumer-protection mechanisms, enforcing age restrictions, and expanding employment opportunities for youth as part of a broader harm-reduction strategy.

articles.title: Building equitable climate adaptation through co-production: a community-engaged, mixed-methods dataset on environmental values and land stewardship in California’s Eastern Sierra Nevada
articles.authors: Paul Berne Burow, Alexander Basaraba, Emma Sage, Natalie Herbert, Jillian Pape, Maxine Gill, Yarrow Syskine, Diana Macias, Miranda Redmond, Ana Bacoch
articles.abstract: The Pinyon Community Climate Action Network (PiCCA) is a community-engaged research initiative designed to evaluate and improve the resilience of communities and ecosystems to climate change in California’s Eastern Sierra Nevada. This co-produced initiative is driven by a transdisciplinary team of research institutions, Tribal Nations, federal land managers, and community-based organizations from across the region. The integrated, mixed-method dataset it generated includes 205 semi-structured interviews, 27 focus groups with 181 participants, and a population-weighted household survey with 1,020 responses. As part of PiCCA, the Eastern Sierra Land and Community Survey (ESLCS) was created to assess cultural, environmental, and landscape values, important places, and stewardship preferences across a broad cross section of the region’s population, in order to inform community-based climate action. PiCCA was created because Tribal Nations and other underserved communities in the region lead adaptation and stewardship work, yet are not consistently engaged by the institutions making adaptation decisions, and their values are not consistently recognized in that decision-making. PiCCA brings together social and ecological research, policy, and practice to build more just approaches to climate adaptation in the Eastern Sierra. It also represents a community-engaged climate action research model for advancing climate justice through knowledge co-production, applied research and policy outputs, and institutional capacity building. The dataset and research model developed through PiCCA contribute to social-ecological systems scholarship by demonstrating how community-engaged approaches grounded in local values, knowledges, and priorities can be adapted to other contexts working toward more just climate adaptation.

articles.title: Framing the Border as a National Security Threat: Fox News Immigration Coverage in the 2016 and 2024 Election Cycles
articles.abstract: While previous scholarship has established the existence of U.S. right-wing ideological media framing and its evolution over time, there is limited research exploring how influential outlets like Fox News have framed immigration across two critical election cycles: 2016 and 2024. These years represent key moments in recent American history, extreme-right-wing media narratives, and how that shapes public perception of emotionally charged topics, such as that of “illegal immigration” in the United States. This research paper explores the question: How has Fox News framed the U.S.–Mexico border and immigration policy during election cycles, particularly in 2016 and 2024? It argues that Fox News strategically frames immigration as a national security threat during the 2016 and 2024 election cycles. I conduct a content analysis of the language, guests, and visuals used on Fox News programming, such as Hannity, to highlight how Fox News deliberately intensified its framing of the U.S.–Mexico border as a national security threat to influence public perception and invoke fear. This paper contributes to the fields of media studies and political communication by providing a multi-year analysis of threat-based storytelling that Fox News uses to shape public opinion. It deepens our understanding of the interplay between media bias, national security threats, and commercial incentives.

articles.title: Demographic Decline and Economic Challenges in East Asia: A Comparative Analysis of the Republic of Korea, Japan, and China
articles.abstract: Although the Republic of Korea, Japan, and China are experiencing similarly rapid fertility decline and population aging, the socioeconomic consequences of these changes differ considerably across the three countries. Population decline does not operate through a single mechanism; rather, its effects are shaped by the structural conditions of households, labor markets, and local economies. Unlike Korea, where demographic anxiety is heavily concentrated in the overheated metropolitan housing market, Japan absorbs its aging burden primarily through a bifurcated labor system. China complicates this regional narrative further. Despite a shrinking national population, the slowing domestic economy is paradoxically struggling to absorb a record influx of university graduates. Across the three countries, unpaid care work remains unevenly distributed between women and men, adding to the pressures surrounding employment, marriage, and family formation. These differences imply that demographic policy cannot rely on a uniform set of incentives. Therefore, policy interventions are more likely to be effective when they respond to the particular institutional and socioeconomic constraints operating within each country.

articles.title: Ecological Sensemaking as a Recursive Process of Indigenous Climate Adaptation: Evidence from the Santal Community of Bangladesh
articles.authors: Sourav Paul Chowdhury, Syed M. Ali Reza, M. Nasim Reza, Dhanno Saha, Md. Solaiman Chowdhury
articles.abstract: Climate adaptation research has focused more on adaptive capacity, technological innovation, and resilience, and less on the interpretive processes that lie before adaptive action. In this study, ecological sensemaking is investigated as a factor influencing agricultural decision-making among the Santal indigenous community in Barind region, which is prone to drought in Bangladesh. The research employed an interpretivist paradigm using thematic analysis of 25 semi-structured interviews. The findings indicate that adaptation starts with the ongoing process of interpreting ecological cues in a way that is negotiated through indigenous ecological knowledge, lived experience, scientific information, and social interaction. Four interrelated themes account for the process of the construction of ecological meanings, their translation to agricultural and livelihood practices, and how they are constrained by structural conditions. The study goes beyond organizational contexts to describe and explain ecological sensemaking, reconceptualizing indigenous ecological knowledge as a process of environmental meaning-making, and proposes a process-based conceptual model for climate adaptation in the face of ecological uncertainty. The study extends Weick's Sensemaking Theory by conceptualizing ecological sensemaking as a recursive, relational, and structurally mediated process operating within Indigenous socio-ecological systems, thereby offering a theoretically grounded understanding of climate adaptation beyond organizational settings.

articles.title: Too Much Detail Kills the Vibe: Quantifying Lyrical Realism and Pop Music Virality
articles.abstract: Pop music songwriters frequently deploy vivid real-world anchors, such as specific vehicle models and city names, to establish narrative realism. However, whether hyper-specific realism systematically drives commercial virality remains an unexamined empirical question. In this paper, we introduce an open-science computational framework that quantifies lyrical realism across 27 tracks from EDM-pop duo The Chainsmokers (2014-2024). By combining Brysbaert psycholinguistic concreteness norms (ILCA), named entity density, VADER sentiment analysis, and sentence embeddings with log-transformed YouTube view counts, we evaluate the structural drivers of pop virality. Statistical analysis reveals a negative rank correlation (Spearman r = -0.632, p < 0.001, 95% Confidence Interval [-0.814, -0.381]) and quadratic regression confirms a concave curvilinear relationship (quadratic beta = -2.18, p = 0.004), providing preliminary evidence consistent with a possible Inverted-U pattern. An estimated candidate optimal concreteness range (ILCA between 2.75 and 2.90) characterizes high-performing crossover tracks, whereas hyper-concreteness (ILCA greater than 3.20) marks a substantial reduction in streaming reach by over-saturating narrative details and restricting listener self-projection. Exploratory TreeSHAP attributions indicate that physical anchors must be balanced with chorus repetition and nostalgic sentiment to optimize streaming reach. All code, figure files, and datasets are open-sourced for computational reproducibility.

articles.title: The Value of Trust: A Note from the Author, Prefacing an Open Research Collection
articles.abstract: Before the formalism, the reason for it. This note argues that trust is the prior human capacity from which language, reason, cooperation, and exchange are built: each of those tools presupposes that words mean tomorrow what they meant today, that another's behavior is predictable enough to act alongside, that a promise made is a promise kept. Trust resists the will - it cannot simply be given or taken by decision - and this resistance is treated as the concept's most important property, one a serious theory must face rather than dismiss. Trust is also the first survival mechanism: the human infant is given only the capacity to attach and to be carried by expectations formed by others, a framework named by Erikson (1950) and grounded in the attachment theory of Bowlby and Ainsworth. The note traces how the same expectation-validation pattern scales from dyads to groups, tribes, institutions, and markets, and motivates the collection's formal program: trust as the measurable relation between an agent's expectations and the validations its environment returns. It states plainly where a formal theory stops: whether trust can ever be willed, and by what mechanism, is a question the theory motivates but does not resolve.

articles.title: Treating the Wounds of Survivors of Sexual Assault on College Campuses
articles.abstract: Sexual assault on college campuses represents one of the most invasive and life-changing types of trauma, occurring at alarming rates across U.S. institutions of higher education. Drawing on national survey data from the 2012 National College Health Assessment (NCHA), as many as one in three college students experience sexual assault. Disparities in prevalence demonstrate that marginalized populations face disproportionate risk, with transgender students, particularly those unsure of their sexual identity (32.6%), identifying as gay or lesbian (20.6%), or identifying as bisexual (18%), experiencing the highest rates of sexual assault, alongside cisgender bisexual women (17%). Racial disparities similarly reveal that Black, Latinx, and mixed-race college students suffer elevated rates of victimization. This paper examines the critical factors influencing disclosure, reporting, and help-seeking behaviors among student survivors, addressing systemic gaps in campus response frameworks. It evaluates trauma-informed clinical interventions and institutional strategies to better support diverse student populations and improve outcomes for survivors of campus sexual violence. Keywords: campus sexual assault, trauma-informed care, Cognitive Processing Therapy, student mental health, health disparities.

articles.title: How analyst choices affect silicon samples from the 2025 CES
articles.abstract: Silicon sampling involves providing a large language model (LLM) with a persona, which is typically some demographic or attitudinal information, then asking a question, and evaluating the response. It has been found to be accurate in some situations and is increasingly used in place of, or as a complement to, evaluations of real humans because it is relatively fast and cheap. Based on data from the 2025 US Cooperative Election Study we systematically evaluate how different AI models, persona detail, news diets, and prompt styles affect synthetic responses. We find that different configurations can cause the share of respondents who support the Democrats to vary across the entire 0 to 100 per cent range. Even if we restrict the configurations to just one model, Democrat support can range from 8 to 100 per cent. The news diet changes the Democrat share by about 10 percentage points unless political identity is included in the persona in which case it has little effect. Our findings motivate the need for disclosure statements to accompany any silicon sample detailing the settings under which it was generated.

articles.title: Vertical kinship distribution at the population level: a Mamushka approximation
articles.abstract: Understanding the population-level distribution of parents, grandparents, and great-grandparents is increasingly important as fertility declines and kin networks thin. However, standard kinship demography tools do not easily capture these distributions when vertical kin are shared across individuals. We introduce a simple approximation to estimate age-specific proportions of women who are childless, mothers, grandmothers, and great-grandmothers from period fertility and mortality schedules. The approach relies on conditional first-order fertility hazards combined with standard age-specific fertility and survival rates, assuming a time-invariant regime and an age-specific distribution of parity. We illustrate the method using Argentine census data and vital statistics, and assess its performance by comparison with a demographic microsimulation. Results show pronounced declines over time in the prevalence of higher-order generational roles, alongside strong subnational heterogeneity. These findings demonstrate how declining fertility reshapes vertical kin availability and provide a tractable tool for studying kinlessness and intergenerational support in population ageing contexts. A key Further development can formally account for heterogeneity across multiple dimensions.

articles.title: Adaptation to International Organizations
articles.abstract: This article examines how international regime complexity affects diplomacy. We argue that diplomats modify their behavior in anticipation of changes to their social environment, driven by psychological pressures to conform rather than learning or socialization. We test this theory of diplomatic adaptation with a natural experiment. Once every four years, states undergo Universal Periodic Review, an assessment of their human rights records at the UN Human Rights Council. Delegates also convene annually for the International Labour Conference to debate the International Labour Organization’s policies. Both events are held at the Palais des Nations in Geneva, many delegates represent their states at both forums, and the timing of UPR was set by lottery. We leverage this lottery and the names of over 37 thousand delegates to assess how exposure to UPR -- at both the state and individual levels -- impacts debate at the ILC. We show that government delegates use human rights language more in ILC debates before UPR and, contra socialization theory, emphasize human rights less often after UPR. These effects are driven by the exposure of individual diplomats to UPR.

articles.title: Contagion or substitution? Experimental evidence on spillovers in trust between legislative and judicial institutions
articles.abstract: Does information about one branch of government affect trust in another? We show that institutional trust is neither institution-specific nor uniformly system-wide. In a survey experiment embedded in the British Election Study Internet Panel, respondents received information about the UK Parliament, the UK Supreme Court, and the European Court of Human Rights that varied the policy content of decisions, party framing of these decisions, and the conduct of individual officeholders. Policy decisions conflicting with respondents' preferences reduce trust well beyond the institution responsible, while congruent decisions leave trust unchanged. Spillovers are strongly asymmetric: parliamentary decisions depress trust in the courts more than in Parliament itself, whereas court decisions produce little spillover beyond the judicial domain. Criticism from parties offsets rather than deepens the penalty, regardless of how much respondents like the cueing party. Information about conduct of officeholders moves trust neither within nor across institutions. We conclude that institutional trust is selectively contagious, shaped above all by the policy decisions institutions make.

articles.title: Peasants and Local Communities: from Cartagena to Yerevan
articles.abstract: This Workin Paper, authored by Carlos Duarte (a member of the United Nations Special Procedures' Working Group of Experts on the Rights of Peasants) explores the relationship between peasantry and local communities across a geographical and social continuum spanning from Cartagena to Yerevan. Supported by the Pontificia Universidad Javeriana in Cali, specifically through its Institute of Intercultural Studies, this work focuses on critical issues of agrarian jurisdiction and land tenure, reflecting rigorous academic inquiry into rural property ownership. Crucially, the text places particular emphasis on the conceptual and legal evolution of "local communities" within the global policy debates surrounding the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Peasants and Other People Working in Rural Areas (UNDROP) and the upcoming COP 17 in Yerevan, Armenia. By analyzing these international instruments, the author highlights the critical role of rural subjects in biodiversity conservation and territorial rights. Additionally, the participation of the Land Observatory (Observatorio de Tierras) emphasizes a technical and analytical framework for territorial governance. Synthetically, the text provides expert insights into the fundamental rights, legal recognition, and social organization of rural populations within diverse international settings.

articles.title: Formulating an equally weighted stock portfolio based on downside risk (Sortino Ratio)
articles.abstract: Investors commonly use historical risk-adjusted performance measures to guide stock choice, yet it remains unclear whether limiting risk analysis to downside volatility only can reliably identify stocks that will deliver increased future returns. This study examined whether the Sortino ratio, a measure of downside risk, can be used to construct a diversified, profit-oriented portfolio that outperforms lower-ranked stocks and market benchmarks. We hypothesized that portfolios comprising the five stocks with the highest Sortino ratios out of a particular sectoral stock pool would generate higher returns from 2015 to 2025 than portfolios comprising of the five stocks with the lowest Sortino ratios of the same. From an initial sample of 179 large, publicly traded U.S companies across six sectors, 141 stocks meeting market capitalization and historical-data requirements were picked and analyzed. Sortino ratios were calculated using monthly returns from the 2011-2014 formation period and the resulting high and low Sortino portfolios were evaluated over ten years. The high-sortino portfolio outperformed low-sortino portfolio by 78.65% at the 10 year mark and both surpassed the S&P 500 and our 141-stock pool. The findings suggest that the Sortino ratio can support long-term stock selection and portfolio construction to an extent. The effectiveness varies by sector and should be utilized in combination with broader company and market specific analysis.

articles.title: Distribution and Compulsion: An Essay on the Distributive Structure of Korean Schools
articles.abstract: Why do students continue to perform educational routines even when they doubt the promises that once justified them? This essay develops a meso-level account of how Korean schools translate social inequality, evaluation, and life-course expectations into everyday action. Following a constructed school year from March to the following February, it treats the episode rather than the person as the basic unit of analysis and reconstructs how background resources shape performance, how performance becomes a marker and qualification, and how qualifications redistribute time, information, trust, recognition, and opportunity. This recurrent linkage is termed distributive grammar. The essay further distinguishes symbolic surplus, through which markers acquire meanings beyond what they directly measure, and distributive self-confirmation, through which evaluation-based resource differences contribute to later differences in performance. The V-Q-C framework separates normative and affective internalization, intersubjective expectations, institutional objectivation, actual efficacy, and capacities for survival, performance, exit, and transition. These relations generate distinct ideal-typical forms of suffering, including suffering within the narrative, double-bind suffering, anomie, structural compulsion, and guilt induced by attacks on legitimacy. The essay argues that continued performance cannot be reduced to either belief or coercion: socially distributed realities teach practical causal relations, while actors’ responses can reproduce or transform those distributions. The framework is presented as an empirically testable research program rather than a completed general theory.

articles.title: From OST (Out-of-School-Time) to Workforce: Building an AI-Ready STEM Pipeline

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This white paper examines how out-of-school-time (OST) STEM programs can be restructured as intentional components of the national workforce development pipeline rather than treated as supplemental enrichment. As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes the skills required for future employment, the paper argues that OST infrastructure represents a largely untapped opportunity to build AI literacy, career-aligned skills, and industry partnerships earlier in students' educational trajectories. Drawing on federal priorities from the U.S. Department of Education, the Department of Labor, and the National Science Foundation, along with legislative context including the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act and the CHIPS and Science Act, the analysis applies four theoretical lenses, the Policy Process Model, Human Capital Theory, Policy Network Theory, and the Multiple Streams Framework, to explain why OST STEM programs remain excluded from formal workforce development policy despite their potential. The paper concludes that the current national focus on AI competitiveness may represent an open policy window, and that formally recognizing OST as workforce infrastructure, paired with targeted investment and cross-sector partnership, is necessary to close the emerging AI-ready workforce gap. Keywords: out-of-school-time programs, STEM education, workforce development policy, AI literacy, policy agenda setting

articles.title: Perkembangan Manajemen Keuangan Syariah: Tren dan Prospek Masa Depan
articles.authors: Julia Alfianti, Yeni Irawan, Anhar Firdaus, Mariana, Diana, Dwi Meilvinasvita
articles.abstract: This study aims to analyze trends, challenges, and opportunities in Islamic financial management, focusing on technological innovation and regulation. The research employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) method, reviewing literature from various academic databases to identify recent developments in Islamic finance. The findings indicate that the growth of Islamic fintech, digitalization, and the adoption of technologies such as blockchain and AI have accelerated the transformation of this industry. However, challenges remain, including unstandardized regulations, low financial literacy, and limited access to Islamic financial services. Therefore, strengthening regulations, enhancing financial literacy, and optimizing digital technology are key factors in driving the sustainable growth of Islamic finance. With the right approach, Islamic finance has the potential to become an integral part of the global financial system.
